Counterfactual World Models:
JEPAs That Reason About “What If”

Randall Balestriero* Brown University AMI Labs   Yann LeCun* New York University AMI Labs Note: Bear et al. [9] use “counterfactual world modeling” for masked prediction in visual perception. Here the term refers to counterfactual outcomes under alternative actions and shared disturbances. Note: For example, when the behavior policy selects actions using only $Z$ and any action randomness is independent of the system’s hidden disturbances. Note: https://github.com/rbalestr-lab/stable-pretraining, revision 9aa93f8b6153.
 github.com/galilai-group/counterfactual-WM   huggingface.co/spaces/galilai-group/cwm_demo
Abstract

World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model’s predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration hh, we prove an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual R2R^{2} from 3838–46%46\% to 8686–96%96\% with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches 9090–94%94\% with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP 2, CLIP and EVA-02, give 8181–95%95\% on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in 3535–69%69\% of events, against 1414–23%23\% for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

1  Introduction

World models predict the consequences of actions and are becoming a core component of agents that interact with the world. From latent dynamics models for control [17, 18, 19, 20, 53, 21] to joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) that predict in the feature space of self-supervised encoders [28, 3, 7, 4, 64, 57], they allow agents to anticipate outcomes before acting.

Yet the real world is never fully observed. Consider the boat of : it picks a heading while an unseen current pushes it. Before acting, no world model can know the current it is about to meet, so the best it can do is predict where the boat ends up on average over currents (green). The observed outcome (diamond) lands elsewhere, and in doing so reveals how far the current actually pushed the boat. A new question then arises: where would the boat have ended up under a different heading, in that same current? (dotted). This is an individual counterfactual. Asked about another heading, a standard world model returns the average over currents again (green) and discards what the outcome revealed. The same question arises whenever a gust of wind or a miscalibrated actuator alters an outcome. Its answer is what one needs to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, to assign credit to an action, and to find in hindsight the action that would have reached the goal, which we call hindsight planning.

This question is fundamentally different from factual prediction: as we prove, a world model trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on its own. A world model learns the conditional consequences of actions from observed transitions, whereas an individual counterfactual asks about an alternative action under the same hidden disturbance. An unpaired factual dataset does not record outcomes under two actions for the same initial state and realized disturbance. Consequently, even a perfect model of factual transitions does not determine how alternative outcomes are coupled, i.e., which outcome under the alternative action belongs to the observed event: distinct counterfactual worlds can induce exactly the same factual distribution ( and ). Neither a more accurate predictor nor a more expressive generative model resolves this ambiguity, and no factual test can reveal it. Without additional structure, individual counterfactuals are not identified.

For many physical systems, nature provides this structure. Natura non facit saltus: nature makes no leaps. When the action and the hidden disturbance enter as separate forces, as the boat’s propulsion and the current do, each changes the state gradually, and each alters the effect of the other only through the change of state it has already caused. Their interaction, i.e., how much the effect of changing the action depends on the disturbance, is therefore second-order in the transition duration. To first order, changing the action changes the outcome by the same amount in every event, and this amount is what a factual world model predicts between the two actions. Separate channels are an assumption on how the disturbance enters, not a consequence of smoothness: a worn actuator whose effect grows with the command is smooth, yet it interacts with the action at first order (), and we test this failure in . Under separate channels, this observation leads to a simple construction. Let zt=f⁡(ot)z_{t}=f(o_{t}) denote the representation of an observation, and let μ⁡(zt,a)\mu(z_{t},a) be a factual world model trained to predict the next representation under action aa. Given an observed transition (zt,at,zt+1)(z_{t},a_{t},z_{t+1}), we estimate the outcome under an alternative action a′a^{\prime} by

z^t+1​(a′)=zt+1+μ⁡(zt,a′)−μ⁡(zt,at).\boxed{\widehat{z}_{t+1}(a^{\prime})=z_{t+1}+\mu(z_{t},a^{\prime})-\mu(z_{t},a_{t}).} (1)

The observed outcome records the effect of the realized disturbance; the world model predicts the effect of changing the action. The construction requires only two evaluations of an ordinary factual predictor and one residual correction: no paired counterfactual data, additional parameters, explicit disturbance inference, or retraining. We call the resulting predictor a counterfactual world model. On the boat of , it shifts the world model’s prediction for the new heading by the drift that the current caused in the observed event (from the green to the orange outline in the bottom-right frame), and follows the true counterfactual (orange against dotted).

In additive worlds, residual reuse is the unique counterfactual rule that is exact for every factual transition (). Outside this regime, its error is governed by the interaction between actions and hidden disturbances, quantified by the mixed derivative of the dynamics (). For short physical transitions with separate action and disturbance channels, this interaction is second-order in the time step hh, leaving only an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) fraction of the disturbance uncertainty unexplained ( and ). This guarantee extends through smooth representations and to systems with hidden velocities (). The rate cannot be uniformly improved: we establish a matching minimax lower bound, with the sharp leading constant, for estimators using unpaired factual transitions and one observed outcome (). Residual reuse therefore achieves the best possible asymptotic rate under the stated information and physical assumptions. How short is short enough depends on the system, and we measure it (). The same analysis identifies the limits of residual reuse: disturbances that scale the command, discontinuous contacts, and folded representations can invalidate it.

Residual correction is familiar in control theory, where disturbance observers, offset-free model predictive control, and iterative learning control reuse errors from observed trajectories [39, 35, 41, 2, 11]. Likewise, additive-noise structural causal models provide a classical route to individual counterfactuals [44, 45]. What has remained unclear is why this construction should be justified for learned world models, what can be recovered without paired counterfactual observations, and whether the principle survives nonlinear representations learned from pixels. Our analysis connects the identification problem of causal inference, the disturbance structure of control, and the representations of modern world models. In particular, factual training of the predictor is sufficient under the stated shared-input conditions, without additional propensity weighting or encoder retraining (, and ).

We test these claims using rendered physical simulators and frozen self-supervised image encoders, DINOv2 [40] in two sizes and masked autoencoders (MAE) [23], and repeat the main comparison with four further frozen encoders, DINOv3 [56], SigLIP 2 [58], CLIP [50] and EVA-02 [16]. We score predicted physical quantities, such as joint angles and positions, by their R2R^{2} against the true counterfactual outcome, i.e., the fraction of its variance they explain (physical counterfactual R2R^{2}). On four environments, with DINOv2 and MAE, counterfactual world models improve physical counterfactual R2R^{2} from 3838–46%46\% to 8686–96%96\% using the same factual predictors, with the correction applied after a readout of these quantities fitted on factual frames; applied to the image features themselves, which needs no state labels, it reaches 7373–94%94\%. On the fifth, the BlueROV2 underwater vehicle, they reach 9090–94%94\% with sixteen times more factual data. They outperform even an oracle predictor that knows the true simulator and its full state, but not the disturbance that occurred, and therefore predicts the average outcome. With the four further encoders, correction after the readout reaches 8181–95%95\% on the first four environments. In hindsight planning, the counterfactual model reaches the goal in 3535–69%69\% of events, compared with 1414–23%23\% for the true-simulator planner without access to the observed outcome. The experiments also recover the predicted failure modes, including contacts, folded coordinates, and disturbances that multiply the command. These results demonstrate that the observed outcome can be more informative for individual counterfactual reasoning than an otherwise perfect predictive model.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    First, we establish the nonidentification of individual counterfactuals from factual world models, including a minimax impossibility result and an explicit gauge ambiguity that persists even with exact factual likelihoods: the latent noise of a generative model can be relabeled separately for each action without changing any factual prediction ().

  • •

    Second, we derive residual reuse from the short-time structure of physical dynamics, prove its exactness under additivity, characterize its interaction error and failure modes, and establish its minimax rate-optimality from unpaired factual data ( and ).

  • •

    Third, we validate the resulting counterfactual world models from pixels, across seven frozen image encoders, physical disturbances, hindsight-planning tasks, and controlled violations of the assumptions ().

2  World Models Need Individual Counterfactuals

World models and causal models describe the same underlying object from different perspectives: how a system responds to actions in the presence of unobserved disturbances. We first distinguish the quantities learned by ordinary world models from the individual counterfactuals needed after observing an outcome (). We then show why individual counterfactuals cannot be identified from factual transitions alone, even by a perfect generative model (). Finally, we identify the additional structure under which counterfactual reasoning becomes possible ().

2.1  World Models Estimate Average Effects, Surprises Ask for Individual Ones

From physical dynamics to world models.

Let sts_{t} denote the physical state of a system, ata_{t} the action applied at time tt, and εt\varepsilon_{t} an unobserved disturbance. The transition obeys

st+1=Fs​(st,at,εt).s_{t+1}=F_{s}(s_{t},a_{t},\varepsilon_{t}). (2)

This single equation admits three interpretations. In control theory, FsF_{s} describes a disturbed dynamical system, or plant. In causal inference, it is a structural causal equation: the action is an intervention, and εt\varepsilon_{t} is the exogenous variable held fixed when constructing a counterfactual [44]. In world modeling, it is the unknown physical mechanism that a learned predictor attempts to approximate. Connections between dynamical systems and structural causal models have been formalized through differential equations [34, 51, 46].

The physical state is generally not observed directly. Instead, an agent receives an observation oto_{t}, such as an image, and represents it through zt=f⁡(ot)z_{t}=f(o_{t}). A representation-based world model learns a predictor μ⁡(zt,at)\mu(z_{t},a_{t}) of the next representation zt+1z_{t+1}. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict in this feature space rather than reconstructing pixels [28]. The encoder can be learned through a joint-embedding objective or obtained from another pretraining method, including one that reconstructs pixels such as a masked autoencoder. Since the world model encodes the frames and predicts in feature space, it is a JEPA either way.

A structural transition zt+1=F⁡(zt,at,εt)z_{t+1}=F(z_{t},a_{t},\varepsilon_{t}) at the representation level requires that ztz_{t} contain sufficient information for the relevant dynamics. This is not automatic: a single image may hide velocity or other state variables. We distinguish the physical mechanism FsF_{s} from its representation-level counterpart and state the required sufficiency assumptions where they are used.

Prediction, intervention, and counterfactuals.

The structural equation supports three distinct queries. Ordinary prediction asks what outcome is likely under the behavior policy that generated the observations, P⁡(st+1∣st)P(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t}). An interventional query asks what would happen if an action were imposed, P⁡(st+1∣st,do⁡(at=a′))P(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},\mathrm{do}(a_{t}=a^{\prime})), averaging over the disturbances that might occur. This is the question answered by an ideal action-conditioned world model before acting. An individual counterfactual asks a different question. Suppose the system executed ata_{t}, experienced a disturbance εt\varepsilon_{t}, and produced the observed outcome st+1s_{t+1}. What would the outcome have been under the alternative action a′a^{\prime}, while the initial state and disturbance remained unchanged? The answer is

st+1​(a′)=Fs​(st,a′,εt),s_{t+1}(a^{\prime})=F_{s}(s_{t},a^{\prime},\varepsilon_{t}),

where εt\varepsilon_{t} is the same disturbance that produced the observed transition. The distinction is essential because an intervention considers possible disturbances, whereas an individual counterfactual concerns the disturbance that actually occurred. In causal terminology, counterfactual reasoning uses the observed outcome to infer information about the realized exogenous variables before changing the action.

From conditional to individual effects.

The distinction can be expressed using potential outcomes. Let Y⁡(a)Y(a) be the outcome that would result under action aa, and let ZZ denote pre-action covariates available to the model. Three quantities are commonly distinguished:

ATE⁡(a′,a)\displaystyle\mathrm{ATE}(a^{\prime},a) =𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a′)−Y⁡(a)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y(a^{\prime})-Y(a)] (average treatment effect),\displaystyle\text{(average treatment effect)}, (3)
CATE⁡(a′,a∣z)\displaystyle\mathrm{CATE}(a^{\prime},a\mid z) =𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a′)−Y⁡(a)∣Z=z]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y(a^{\prime})-Y(a)\mid Z=z] (conditional average treatment effect),\displaystyle\text{(conditional average treatment effect)}, (4)
ITEi​(a′,a)\displaystyle\mathrm{ITE}_{i}(a^{\prime},a) =Yi​(a′)−Yi​(a)\displaystyle=Y_{i}(a^{\prime})-Y_{i}(a) (individual treatment effect).\displaystyle\text{(individual treatment effect)}. (5)

The ATE averages over the population, the CATE averages over events sharing the same pre-action information, and the ITE concerns one particular event. Estimating conditional effects from observations is a central problem in causal representation learning and treatment-effect estimation [54, 29, 10, 32]. To connect these definitions to a world model, suppose actions are conditionally exchangeable given the model input ZZ, i.e., once ZZ is known, the action taken carries no further information about the potential outcomes (no hidden confounding). Suppose also that actions have sufficient overlap, i.e., the logged actions cover every queried action at every value of ZZ. Under these conditions, squared-loss prediction of YY from (Z,A)(Z,A) identifies the conditional interventional mean

μ⁡(z,a)=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(a)∣Z=z].\mu(z,a)=\mathbb{E}[Y(a)\mid Z=z].

Consequently, evaluating the predictor at two actions gives

μ⁡(z,a′)−μ⁡(z,a)=CATE⁡(a′,a∣z).\mu(z,a^{\prime})-\mu(z,a)=\mathrm{CATE}(a^{\prime},a\mid z).

Without these conditions, a factual predictor instead learns an observational conditional mean, which can differ from the conditional interventional mean. We return to the relevant shared-input conditions in and .

Even when the conditional interventional means are identified exactly, they do not determine the individual effect. The CATE averages over disturbances compatible with Z=zZ=z, while the ITE compares two outcomes under the same realized disturbance. Equivalently, the ATE and CATE depend on marginal distributions of potential outcomes, whereas the ITE depends on how those outcomes are coupled across actions, i.e., on their joint distribution, which says which outcome under a′a^{\prime} belongs to the same event as a given outcome under aa. This missing coupling is the fundamental obstacle to individual counterfactual world modeling.

Individual and average effects differ only through interaction.

We say that the action and the disturbance interact when the effect of changing the action depends on which disturbance occurred. Without interaction, the ITE is the same in every event and therefore equals the CATE; with interaction, the two differ by an amount set by the unobserved disturbance. For the boat of , a uniform current would drift the boat by the same amount whatever its heading, so turning would move the boat’s position by the same amount in every event, and its counterfactual position would be the observed one plus the CATE. Its current varies slowly in space, so the drift depends only slightly on where the boat goes, and the interaction is small; measures how it grows as the eddies shrink. A worn actuator that delivers only a fraction of the command is the opposite case: how far a larger command moves the system depends on the wear, so no single correction is right for every event. Interaction is what separates the coupling from a plain shift: without it, the coupling reduces to a shift by the CATE, which factual data identify, and the interaction measures how far the true coupling departs from that shift. Factual data alone cannot tell the two cases apart: the two mechanisms of the next subsection () share their factual laws, yet the first has no interaction and the second does. shows when physics keeps the interaction small.

2.2  No Factual World Model Identifies Individual Counterfactuals

Can a sufficiently accurate or expressive world model recover the missing coupling and estimate individual treatment effects? In general, it cannot. Unpaired factual data reveal the outcome distribution associated with each action, but do not record outcomes under two actions for the same realized disturbance. We first establish that this ambiguity persists with infinite data, even under perfect generative world modeling.

Factual marginals do not determine counterfactuals.

Consider the potential outcomes Y⁡(a)Y(a) and Y⁡(a′)Y(a^{\prime}). An arbitrarily large factual dataset can identify their marginal laws (we write law for the probability distribution of a random variable) under the appropriate identification and coverage conditions. It does not, however, reveal their joint law. Different joint distributions can share exactly the same marginals while assigning different outcomes to the same individual under alternative actions. For example, let UU be uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1]. Consider two mechanisms with the same outcome under action aa,

Y⁡(a)=U,Y(a)=U,

but different outcomes under a′a^{\prime}:

Y⁡(a′)=UorY⁡(a′)=1−U.Y(a^{\prime})=U\qquad\text{or}\qquad Y(a^{\prime})=1-U.

In both mechanisms, the outcome is uniformly distributed under either action. Their factual and interventional distributions are therefore identical. Yet observing Y⁡(a)=uY(a)=u gives counterfactual outcomes uu and 1−u1-u, respectively; neither factual distribution distinguishes the two. The following proposition states why these marginals do not identify individual treatment effects.

Proposition 2.1 (Marginals do not identify counterfactual matchings).

Two structural models can agree on every action-conditional outcome law while predicting different alternatives for the same observed transition. (Proof in .)

The ambiguity is not due to limited data, imperfect optimization, or insufficient model capacity. Even when all interventional laws are known exactly, the minimax risk for estimating an individual counterfactual remains bounded away from zero, as does that of the individual treatment effect ( and ). The two mechanisms can also be smooth; smoothness of the factual outcome laws alone does not identify their coupling. This is an instance of the causal hierarchy separating interventions from counterfactuals [8], and of the classical nonidentification of the joint distribution of potential outcomes from experimental marginals [24]. A deterministic world model predicting the conditional mean therefore cannot recover the individual counterfactual merely by becoming more accurate. But perhaps a generative world model could do better, by sampling a latent disturbance and reusing it under another action. The next result shows why factual training does not identify this operation either.

Perfect generative models still leave the coupling free.

Suppose the factual outcome law at state ss and action aa is represented as the push-forward

Ps,a=(Ts,a)#​ν,P_{s,a}=(T_{s,a})_{\#}\nu,

where ν\nu is a reference noise distribution and Ts,aT_{s,a} is a measurable bijection. That is, an outcome is generated by drawing noise from ν\nu and passing it through Ts,aT_{s,a}; Ps,aP_{s,a} is the resulting law of the outcome, the push-forward of ν\nu by Ts,aT_{s,a}. An invertible generative model can infer the latent noise associated with an observed outcome yy through Ts,a−1​(y)T_{s,a}^{-1}(y) and decode it under an alternative action a′a^{\prime}. Its implied counterfactual is thus the composition (∘\circ) of these two maps,

Ts,a′∘Ts,a−1​(y).T_{s,a^{\prime}}\circ T_{s,a}^{-1}(y).

This appears to solve the individual counterfactual problem: infer the noise from what happened, then reuse it to predict what would have happened. The difficulty is that the inferred noise has no uniquely identified correspondence across actions. Consider any family of ν\nu-preserving bijections Gs,aG_{s,a}. Reparameterizing the noise separately for each action leaves the factual laws unchanged, but can change the counterfactual mapping, as we formalize below.

Theorem 2.2 (Factual gauge nonidentification).

Let Ps,a=(Ts,a)#​νP_{s,a}=(T_{s,a})_{\#}\nu with measurable bijections Ts,aT_{s,a}. For every measurable family of ν\nu-preserving bijections Gs,aG_{s,a}, the mechanisms

T~s,a=Ts,a∘Gs,a\widetilde{T}_{s,a}=T_{s,a}\circ G_{s,a}

induce exactly the same factual laws, but their counterfactual coupling is

T~s,a′∘T~s,a−1=Ts,a′∘Gs,a′∘Gs,a−1∘Ts,a−1.\widetilde{T}_{s,a^{\prime}}\circ\widetilde{T}_{s,a}^{-1}=T_{s,a^{\prime}}\circ G_{s,a^{\prime}}\circ G_{s,a}^{-1}\circ T_{s,a}^{-1}.

Factual likelihood, calibration, or any criterion depending only on {Ps,a}\{P_{s,a}\} therefore cannot identify the same-disturbance counterfactual. The gauge cancels when it is action-independent. Within the class of invertible transports from the common reference law, every factual-law-preserving reparameterization is of this form.

(Proof in .)

The theorem identifies the precise missing information: factual training constrains the distribution of latent noise at each action, but not how a particular realization of that noise corresponds across actions. This is an action-dependent gauge freedom, a term borrowed from physics for a change of description, here a relabeling of the noise, that leaves every observable prediction unchanged. The freedom is real whenever ν\nu admits a ν\nu-preserving bijection other than the identity, as any continuous noise law does, e.g., through a reflection of a centered Gaussian; only deterministic dynamics, with ν\nu a point mass, leave nothing to relabel. A normalizing flow with an exact likelihood can infer a latent variable from an observed transition, yet factual data alone do not establish that this latent variable represents the same physical disturbance under a different action. Related nonidentification results for bijective causal models appear in Nasr-Esfahany et al. [37], Nasr-Esfahany and Kiciman [36]; see also neural causal models in Xia et al. [62]. The same limitation applies beyond invertible generators. A diffusion or latent-variable world model may sample realistic outcomes under alternative actions, but its factual objective does not, by itself, determine which alternative outcome corresponds to the particular event that was observed. Individual counterfactuals therefore require information about the correspondence across actions that factual predictive accuracy does not measure.

2.3  Every Counterfactual Needs Structure Beyond Factual Data

The preceding results establish a boundary between learning factual distributions and identifying individual counterfactuals. Factual data can identify interventional quantities under the appropriate assumptions, but the coupling between potential outcomes requires additional structure. This structure may come from paired observations, a known mechanism, restrictions on the disturbance, or assumptions on how actions affect the system.

How existing methods resolve the ambiguity.

Different approaches to counterfactual reasoning provide the missing coupling in different ways. Structural causal models impose restrictions on how exogenous variables generate outcomes [44, 45]. Additive-noise models provide an especially simple case: the observed residual identifies the disturbance contribution, which can then be reused under a different action [26]. Monotone scalar responses identify counterfactuals through rank preservation: if a scalar outcome increases with a scalar disturbance under every action, an event keeps its quantile in the outcome distribution across actions, so the counterfactual is the outcome at the same quantile under a′a^{\prime} (rank transport). Suitable bijective mechanisms can support more general transport constructions [14, 5, 37, 61]. Alternatively, paired observations or a known simulator can provide the correspondence between actions directly [6, 27, 12, 38, 43].

Counterfactual reasoning has also been studied in reinforcement learning and world modeling, including data augmentation [30, 47, 48], credit assignment [33], explanation [60], and counterfactual action-sequence optimization [59, 22]. Observed trajectory residuals have been reused to correct model errors in model-based control [1]. More recent approaches study counterfactual prediction in driving world models through abduction, action, and prediction [63], noise-coupled branching in interactive video world models [31], and action-discriminative latent models for counterfactual model predictive control [49]. These works differ in their assumptions, supervision, and target counterfactual queries, but share (i) the need for some correspondence between alternative outcomes, (ii) expert knowledge in some structural model, or (iii) access to simulators for paired data generation.

In practice, the coupling is the hard requirement.

Exchangeability and overlap hold whenever the logged actions depend only on what the world model sees, plus independent exploration that covers the queried actions (); an operator who perceives more than is recorded can break them. The coupling requirements of are harder to meet. Paired outcomes and known mechanisms are rarely available outside simulation, and factual data can never confirm additivity or rank preservation, since the coupling they assert is not identified (). We therefore do not postulate additivity itself: derives it, up to second order, from one physical assumption, separate action and disturbance channels, with an explicit error bound, and tests where it breaks.

Physical dynamics constrain counterfactual outcomes.

Physical dynamics can constrain the correspondence between outcomes under different actions without learning it or using a known simulator. When actions and disturbances enter through separate force-like channels, the effect of changing an action is approximately independent of the realized disturbance over a sufficiently short transition. The approximation error is governed by their interaction, rather than by the magnitude of the disturbance itself. This distinction matters for learned world models. Instead of attempting to infer the true exogenous variable or identify a generative coupling from factual data, we can reuse the discrepancy between the observed outcome and the factual prediction. The world model then provides only the change attributable to the alternative action. The resulting counterfactual depends on an observable residual and two ordinary predictions, not on a learned correspondence between latent noise variables.

The next section formalizes this principle. We first establish why residual reuse is exact in additive systems, then quantify the error introduced by action–disturbance interactions. Finally, we show that the short-time structure of physical dynamics controls this interaction and that the resulting approximation achieves the minimax-optimal rate from unpaired factual data ().

3  Natura Non Facit Saltus: Counterfactuals from a World Without Leaps

The previous section established that factual transition laws do not identify individual counterfactuals (). Identification requires additional structure on how the same disturbance affects outcomes under different actions. Here we consider physical dynamics in which actions and disturbances enter through separate force-like channels. Their effects add in the instantaneous dynamics, while their interaction accumulates over time. We first derive residual reuse and characterize its exactness under additive responses. We then express its error in terms of the action–disturbance interaction. For smooth physical systems, this interaction is second-order in the transition duration, yielding a minimax-optimal counterfactual approximation. Finally, we establish the conditions under which a factual world model trained by squared loss provides the required action contrast.

3.1  Residual Reuse for Individual Counterfactuals

Consider an observed transition (Ht,at,zt+1)(H_{t},a_{t},z_{t+1}), where HtH_{t} contains the current observation embedding and, optionally, past embeddings and actions. Let μ⁡(Ht,a)\mu(H_{t},a) predict the next embedding under action aa. The counterfactual model uses the observed outcome and the predicted difference between the factual and alternative actions.

Definition 3.1 (Counterfactual world model).

Given a factual predictor μ\mu and an observed transition (Ht,at,zt+1)(H_{t},a_{t},z_{t+1}), the counterfactual world model estimates the outcome under action a′a^{\prime} by

z^t+1​(a′)=zt+1+μ⁡(Ht,a′)−μ⁡(Ht,at).\widehat{z}_{t+1}(a^{\prime})=z_{t+1}+\mu(H_{t},a^{\prime})-\mu(H_{t},a_{t}). (6)

For a frozen readout π\pi mapping embeddings to physical quantities, we may instead apply the correction in the readout coordinates:

s^t+1​(a′)=π⁡(zt+1)+π⁡(μ⁡(Ht,a′))−π⁡(μ⁡(Ht,at)).\widehat{s}_{t+1}(a^{\prime})=\pi(z_{t+1})+\pi(\mu(H_{t},a^{\prime}))-\pi(\mu(H_{t},a_{t})). (7)

An alternative is to decode the transported embedding, π⁡(z^t+1​(a′))\pi(\widehat{z}_{t+1}(a^{\prime})). The two constructions generally differ when π\pi is nonlinear. A nonlinear readout can introduce error even when the factual prediction μ\mu is exact, so guarantees in readout coordinates also require control of the error in the decoded action contrast.

illustrates the rule. Both constructions use the factual predictor without retraining but differ in the coordinates in which the residual is transported. As shown below, these coordinates determine the size of the counterfactual approximation error. They also differ in what they need: () uses only the encoder and the factual predictor, and therefore applies to any pretrained representation, whereas () needs a readout fitted on physical-state labels of factual frames, in exchange for coordinates in which the interaction can be much smaller (). To analyze the rule, fix a source representation zz and a transition duration h>0h>0 and denote by Yh​(a)=Fh​(z,a,ε)Y_{h}(a)=F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon) the outcome under action aa and realized disturbance ε\varepsilon. Counterfactual outcomes Yh​(a)Y_{h}(a) and Yh​(a′)Y_{h}(a^{\prime}) are defined using the same ε\varepsilon. Assume that the disturbance has a common conditional law νz\nu_{z} across actions, and that the queried actions have factual support. The population squared-loss predictor is then μh​(z,a)=𝔼νz​[Fh​(z,a,ε)]\mu_{h}(z,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}[F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)]. The required identification conditions for learning this mean from factual transitions are given in . Given the observed outcome y=Yh​(a)y=Y_{h}(a), define residual reuse with the exact factual predictions

TR​(z,a,y,a′)=y+μh​(z,a′)−μh​(z,a).T_{R}(z,a,y,a^{\prime})=y+\mu_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-\mu_{h}(z,a). (8)

The correction keeps the factual residual y−μh​(z,a)y-\mu_{h}(z,a) and adds it to the predicted outcome under a′a^{\prime}. In causal inference, this is the counterfactual construction associated with an additive-noise model [44, 45]. In control, related residual corrections appear in disturbance observers and offset-free control [35, 41]. Let Δh=Yh​(a′)−Yh​(a)\Delta_{h}=Y_{h}(a^{\prime})-Y_{h}(a) be the individual action contrast, i.e., the change in outcome caused by switching from aa to a′a^{\prime} in the same event. Since μh​(z,a′)−μh​(z,a)=𝔼νz​Δh\mu_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-\mu_{h}(z,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\Delta_{h}, substitution into () gives the exact identity

TR−Yh​(a′)\displaystyle T_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime}) =𝔼νz​Δh−Δh,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\Delta_{h}-\Delta_{h}, (9)
𝔼νz​‖TR−Yh​(a′)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|T_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|^{2} =tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δh).\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta_{h}). (10)

Here 𝔼νz\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}} averages over the disturbance ε∼νz\varepsilon\sim\nu_{z}, Varνz\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}} is the covariance matrix under that law (written Covνz\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{z}} for ε\varepsilon itself), and tr\operatorname{tr} is the matrix trace, so tr⁡Varνz\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}} sums the variances of all coordinates. The residual-reuse error is therefore the variance of the individual action effect across disturbances, i.e., of the gap between the ITE and the CATE of . In particular, residual reuse is exact for a fixed action pair if and only if the action contrast is independent of the disturbance, up to νz\nu_{z}-null sets. Consider an additive response

Fh​(z,a,ε)=mh​(z,a)+qh​(z,ε).F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)=m_{h}(z,a)+q_{h}(z,\varepsilon). (11)

The same disturbance term appears under both actions, so Δh=mh​(z,a′)−mh​(z,a)\Delta_{h}=m_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-m_{h}(z,a) is independent of ε\varepsilon, giving TR=Yh​(a′)T_{R}=Y_{h}(a^{\prime}) for every realized transition, even if qhq_{h} is nonlinear, multidimensional, or noninjective.

The observed residual identifies the disturbance contribution needed for the counterfactual: y−μh​(z,a)=qh​(z,ε)−𝔼νz​qh​(z,ε)y-\mu_{h}(z,a)=q_{h}(z,\varepsilon)-\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}q_{h}(z,\varepsilon). Since this centered contribution is shared across actions, we can reuse it without recovering ε\varepsilon or learning qhq_{h}. Even when several disturbances produce the same observed outcome, they all give the same action contrast, so the counterfactual remains identified although the disturbance itself is not.

Proposition 3.2 (Residual reuse is the only rule exact in every additive world).

Let T⁡(z,a,y,a′)T(z,a,y,a^{\prime}) be any counterfactual rule computed from the factual laws and an observed transition. If TT is exact in every world with an additive response

Fh​(z,a,ε)=mh​(z,a)+qh​(z,ε),F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)=m_{h}(z,a)+q_{h}(z,\varepsilon),

a common disturbance law and supported queries, then in each such world

T⁡(z,a,y,a′)=y+μh​(z,a′)−μh​(z,a)T(z,a,y,a^{\prime})=y+\mu_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-\mu_{h}(z,a)

for every supported action pair and every observed outcome yy.

(Proof in .)

Thus, additive structure identifies an individual counterfactual from factual conditional means and one observed outcome, without identifying a latent disturbance or a generative coupling. The next result quantifies the error when the action contrast depends on the disturbance.

3.2  Counterfactual Error Is Controlled by Action–Disturbance Interactions

The preceding subsection established that residual reuse is exact in additive worlds and is the only rule with that guarantee. We now quantify its error beyond additivity: by (10), the error is the variation of the action contrast across disturbances, i.e., the action–disturbance interaction of , which we bound through the mixed action–disturbance derivative of the transition map.

Fix a source zz and suppress the fixed duration hh in the notation. Let 𝒜⊆ℝp\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} and 𝒰⊆ℝm\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} be closed convex sets containing the supported actions and the support of νz\nu_{z}, with 𝔼νz​‖ε‖2<∞\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|\varepsilon\|^{2}<\infty.

Suppose F⁡(z,a,ε)F(z,a,\varepsilon) is continuously differentiable in ε\varepsilon, ∂εF\partial_{\varepsilon}F is continuously differentiable in aa, and the mixed derivative satisfies

‖∂a∂εF⁡(z,a,ε)​[u,v]‖≤Kz​‖u‖​‖v‖\bigl\|\partial_{a}\partial_{\varepsilon}F(z,a,\varepsilon)[u,v]\bigr\|\leq K_{z}\|u\|\|v\| (12)

for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, ε∈𝒰\varepsilon\in\mathcal{U} and directions u,vu,v.

Theorem 3.3 (Interaction bound).

Under these conditions, every supported action pair satisfies

𝔼νz​‖TR−Y⁡(a′)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|T_{R}-Y(a^{\prime})\|^{2} =tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δ)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta) (13)
≤Kz2​‖a′−a‖2​tr⁡Covνz⁡(ε).\displaystyle\leq K_{z}^{2}\|a^{\prime}-a\|^{2}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{z}}(\varepsilon).

If, in addition, the response under a′a^{\prime} separates disturbances,

‖F⁡(z,a′,ε)−F⁡(z,a′,ε′)‖≥κz​‖ε−ε′‖,κz>0,\|F(z,a^{\prime},\varepsilon)-F(z,a^{\prime},\varepsilon^{\prime})\|\geq\kappa_{z}\|\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{\prime}\|,\qquad\kappa_{z}>0,

then, whenever the disturbance variance is nonzero,

ρz​(a,a′):=tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δ)tr⁡Varνz⁡(Y⁡(a′))≤(Kz​‖a′−a‖κz)2.\rho_{z}(a,a^{\prime}):=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta)}{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y(a^{\prime}))}\leq\left(\frac{K_{z}\|a^{\prime}-a\|}{\kappa_{z}}\right)^{2}. (14)

(Proof in .)

The separation condition gives tr⁡Varνz⁡(Y⁡(a′))≥κz2​tr​Covνz⁡(ε)\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y(a^{\prime}))\geq\kappa_{z}^{2}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{z}}(\varepsilon), yielding the relative bound. The mixed derivative measures how the response to a disturbance changes with the action. When it vanishes, the action contrast is disturbance-independent and residual reuse is exact. When it is small, the counterfactual error is controlled even if the disturbance itself is large. The normalized quantity ρz​(a,a′)\rho_{z}(a,a^{\prime}) compares residual reuse with an ideal predictor that does not observe the factual outcome. Indeed, the minimum squared risk of predicting Y⁡(a′)Y(a^{\prime}) from zz and a′a^{\prime} alone is

infc𝔼νz​‖c−Y⁡(a′)‖2=tr⁡Varνz⁡(Y⁡(a′)).\inf_{c}\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|c-Y(a^{\prime})\|^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y(a^{\prime})).

The numerator of ρz\rho_{z} is the risk of residual reuse with exact factual predictions. Therefore,

ρz<1⟺residual reuse improves on the exact factual predictor.\rho_{z}<1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{residual reuse improves on the exact factual predictor}.

At ρz=0\rho_{z}=0 the counterfactual is exact; at ρz>1\rho_{z}>1 the residual correction is worse than ignoring the observed outcome. The bound also identifies the relevant dimensionless quantity, Kz​‖a′−a‖κz\frac{K_{z}\|a^{\prime}-a\|}{\kappa_{z}}. A small mixed derivative is not sufficient on its own: the outcome must also distinguish disturbances, as quantified by κz\kappa_{z}. In particular, a representation that suppresses first-order disturbance variation may have a small denominator in () even when the underlying physical dynamics are smooth.

This coordinate dependence motivates transporting the residual after a physical readout, as in ().

A learned predictor contributes error only through its action contrast: errors shared by the factual and alternative predictions cancel. To separate this estimation error from the physical interaction, let

μ^​(z,a)=μ⁡(z,a)+e⁡(z,a)\widehat{\mu}(z,a)=\mu(z,a)+e(z,a)

and write

eΔ​(z,a,a′)=e⁡(z,a′)−e⁡(z,a).e_{\Delta}(z,a,a^{\prime})=e(z,a^{\prime})-e(z,a).

For a fitted predictor fixed independently of the query disturbance,

T^R−Y⁡(a′)\displaystyle\widehat{T}_{R}-Y(a^{\prime}) =TR−Y⁡(a′)+eΔ​(z,a,a′),\displaystyle=T_{R}-Y(a^{\prime})+e_{\Delta}(z,a,a^{\prime}), (15)
𝔼νz​‖T^R−Y⁡(a′)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|\widehat{T}_{R}-Y(a^{\prime})\|^{2} =tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δ)+‖eΔ​(z,a,a′)‖2.\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta)+\|e_{\Delta}(z,a,a^{\prime})\|^{2}. (16)

With exact factual predictions, the residual-reuse error has zero mean, so its cross term with the fixed error in the predicted action contrast vanishes. Equation (16) therefore separates the error due to the physical interaction from that due to learning the action contrast; for a predictor fitted on random training data, the identity holds conditional on that fit whenever the query disturbance still follows νz\nu_{z}.

What factual data reveal about the interaction.

The ratio ρz\rho_{z} depends on the same-event contrast Δ\Delta, and therefore on the coupling that factual data do not identify (). Computing it requires paired outcomes, from a simulator or from trials that repeat a persistent disturbance. In our experiments, it is an evaluation diagnostic computed from simulator outcomes (), not a quantity available before deployment. Factual data bound it only from below. The true joint law of the two centered outcomes Y⁡(a)−𝔼νz​Y​(a)Y(a)-\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}Y(a) and Y⁡(a′)−𝔼νz​Y​(a′)Y(a^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}Y(a^{\prime}) is one coupling of their laws, so tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δ)\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta) is at least the smallest mean squared distance between two random vectors with these laws (the squared Wasserstein distance), and, by the reverse triangle inequality, at least

(tr⁡Varνz⁡(Y⁡(a′))−tr⁡Varνz⁡(Y⁡(a)))2.\Bigl(\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y(a^{\prime}))}-\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y(a))}\Bigr)^{2}.

Both bounds involve only factual laws; the second needs only the expected squared residual of a factual world model under each action, which a second regression on factual data estimates. An outcome spread that changes with the action, as under a gain fault with commands of different magnitudes, therefore flags a large interaction from factual data alone. The converse fails: in the mechanism Y⁡(a)=UY(a)=U, Y⁡(a′)=1−UY(a^{\prime})=1-U of , both centered laws are uniform on [−12,12][-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}], so both bounds vanish, yet ρz=4\rho_{z}=4. Certifying a small interaction therefore needs another source of information: where the disturbance enters (), a simulator, or paired trials.

The interaction bound controls tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δ)\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta). We next show why this variance is small for short physical transitions.

3.3  Physical Dynamics Yield Minimax-Optimal Counterfactuals

Residual reuse is exact under additivity, and the interaction bound quantifies its error beyond that regime. In physical systems, the principle behind our title, natura non facit saltus (nature makes no leaps), takes a concrete form: separate action and disturbance forces accumulate over time and interact only through subsequent changes of state. This yields approximate additivity over a short transition, with a counterfactual error rate that we prove is minimax optimal given unpaired factual data and one observed outcome. In Newtonian and Lagrangian mechanics, this separate-force structure takes the form

M⁡(q)​q¨=τa​(q,a)+τε​(q,q˙,ε)−c⁡(q,q˙).M(q)\ddot{q}=\tau_{a}(q,a)+\tau_{\varepsilon}(q,\dot{q},\varepsilon)-c(q,\dot{q}). (17)

Here qq denotes configuration, M⁡(q)M(q) the mass matrix, τa\tau_{a} and τε\tau_{\varepsilon} the action and disturbance forces, and cc the remaining mechanical terms; dots denote time derivatives, so q˙\dot{q} is the velocity and q¨\ddot{q} the acceleration. At a fixed position and velocity, the two force contributions add; their interaction arises as the action changes the state at which the disturbance acts, and conversely. This separate-channel structure is assumed, not derived from smoothness: the worn actuator of is smooth yet interacts with the action at first order, and we list it among the violations at the end of this subsection.

To formalize this, consider the continuous-time system, an ordinary differential equation (ODE),

s˙=vs​(s,a)+bs​(s,ε),z=ℰ⁡(s)=f⁡(o⁡(s)),\dot{s}=v_{s}(s,a)+b_{s}(s,\varepsilon),\qquad z=\mathcal{E}(s)=f(o(s)), (18)

with action and disturbance held fixed over a transition of duration hh. The observation o⁡(s)o(s) is encoded by the same frozen encoder ff used throughout; ℰ=f∘o\mathcal{E}=f\circ o denotes their composition so that derivatives with respect to the physical state ss are explicit.

For a sufficiently smooth vector field, Taylor expansion gives

st+h=st+h⁡[vs​(st,a)+bs​(st,ε)]+O⁡(h2).s_{t+h}=s_{t}+h\bigl[v_{s}(s_{t},a)+b_{s}(s_{t},\varepsilon)\bigr]+O(h^{2}). (19)

The first-order effect of the action does not depend on the disturbance, and the first-order effect of the disturbance does not depend on the action. Their interaction enters through higher-order terms.

Applying the smooth composition ℰ=f∘o\mathcal{E}=f\circ o gives the corresponding expansion in representation coordinates,

zt+h=zt+h​D​ℰ​(st)​vs​(st,a)+h​D​ℰ​(st)​bs​(st,ε)+O⁡(h2).z_{t+h}=z_{t}+hD\mathcal{E}(s_{t})v_{s}(s_{t},a)+hD\mathcal{E}(s_{t})b_{s}(s_{t},\varepsilon)+O(h^{2}).

Here D​ℰ​(st)D\mathcal{E}(s_{t}) is the Jacobian of ℰ\mathcal{E} at sts_{t}, which maps a small change of physical state to the resulting change of embedding. The additive action and disturbance terms in the physical dynamics remain separate at first order after applying the smooth map ℰ\mathcal{E}, regardless of the encoder pretraining objective. The representation must still contain enough information to determine these first-order responses; conditioning on an insufficient ztz_{t} can invalidate the expansion.

The following theorem states the property directly for the transition map. It collects all terms beyond first order into a remainder RhR_{h} and assumes that its root-mean-square size over disturbances, ‖Rh‖L2​(νz)=(𝔼νz​‖Rh‖2)1/2\|R_{h}\|_{L^{2}(\nu_{z})}=(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|R_{h}\|^{2})^{1/2}, is at most C​h2Ch^{2} for a constant CC that does not depend on hh.

Theorem 3.4 (Short-time residual counterfactuals).

Assume, uniformly on the supported source/action domain, that

Fh​(z,a,ε)=z+h​v​(z,a)+h​w​(z,ε)+Rh​(z,a,ε),‖Rh​(z,a,ε)‖L2​(νz)≤C​h2,F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)=z+h\,v(z,a)+h\,w(z,\varepsilon)+R_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon),\qquad\|R_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)\|_{L^{2}(\nu_{z})}\leq Ch^{2}, (20)

with all terms square integrable and a common disturbance law νz\nu_{z} across actions.

Then, for every supported action pair,

‖TR−Yh​(a′)‖L2​(νz)≤2​C​h2,𝔼νz​‖TR−Yh​(a′)‖2≤4​C2​h4.\|T_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|_{L^{2}(\nu_{z})}\leq 2Ch^{2},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|T_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|^{2}\leq 4C^{2}h^{4}. (21)

For a fixed fitted predictor μ^h=μh+eh\widehat{\mu}_{h}=\mu_{h}+e_{h},

‖T^R−Yh​(a′)‖L2​(νz)≤2​C​h2+‖eh​(z,a′)−eh​(z,a)‖.\|\widehat{T}_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|_{L^{2}(\nu_{z})}\leq 2Ch^{2}+\|e_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-e_{h}(z,a)\|. (22)

(Proof in .)

The cancellation follows directly from the action contrast. Subtracting the expansions under aa and a′a^{\prime} gives

Δh\displaystyle\Delta_{h} =Fh​(z,a′,ε)−Fh​(z,a,ε)\displaystyle=F_{h}(z,a^{\prime},\varepsilon)-F_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon) (23)
=h⁡[v⁡(z,a′)−v⁡(z,a)]+Rh​(z,a′,ε)−Rh​(z,a,ε).\displaystyle=h\bigl[v(z,a^{\prime})-v(z,a)\bigr]+R_{h}(z,a^{\prime},\varepsilon)-R_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon). (24)

The first-order disturbance term h​w​(z,ε)h\,w(z,\varepsilon) cancels. Consequently,

tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δh)=O⁡(h4),\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta_{h})=O(h^{4}),

which gives the squared-error rate through (10).

For (), the expansion follows from Taylor’s formula when the vector fields are continuously differentiable, ℰ\mathcal{E} is twice continuously differentiable, and the relevant derivative and moment bounds hold uniformly (). The corresponding terms are

v⁡(z,a)=D​ℰ​(s)​vs​(s,a),w⁡(z,ε)=D​ℰ​(s)​bs​(s,ε).v(z,a)=D\mathcal{E}(s)v_{s}(s,a),\qquad w(z,\varepsilon)=D\mathcal{E}(s)b_{s}(s,\varepsilon).

This covers force-like disturbances with separate action and disturbance channels, including temporally persistent disturbances when conditioned on an appropriate source context.

The absolute error rate does not by itself establish the value of conditioning on the observed outcome. As h→0h\to 0, all outcomes approach their source state, so even predictors that ignore both the action and disturbance can have small absolute error (). We therefore consider the interaction ratio relative to the disturbance-induced variance.

Corollary 3.5 (Residual reuse explains all but an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) fraction).

Under , suppose the first-order disturbance effect separates disturbances:

‖w⁡(z,ε)−w⁡(z,ε′)‖≥κ​‖ε−ε′‖,\|w(z,\varepsilon)-w(z,\varepsilon^{\prime})\|\geq\kappa\|\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{\prime}\|,

with κ>0\kappa>0, and let

σ2=tr⁡Covνz⁡(ε)>0.\sigma^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{z}}(\varepsilon)>0.

For h<κ​σ/(2​C)h<\kappa\sigma/(\sqrt{2}\,C),

ρh​(a,a′)=𝔼νz​‖TR−Yh​(a′)‖2tr⁡Varνz⁡(Yh​(a′))≤(2​C​hκ​σ−2​C​h)2=O⁡(h2).\rho_{h}(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|T_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|^{2}}{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(Y_{h}(a^{\prime}))}\leq\left(\frac{2Ch}{\kappa\sigma-\sqrt{2}\,Ch}\right)^{2}=O(h^{2}). (25)

(Proof in .)

The numerator is O⁡(h4)O(h^{4}) by , while the disturbance-induced variance in the denominator is of order h2h^{2} under the separation condition. Hence the relative risk decreases as h2h^{2}. This is the relevant guarantee: residual reuse removes an increasing fraction of the disturbance uncertainty as the transition duration decreases. The corollary says how fast the error vanishes, not how short is short enough. Its bound holds only below the duration stated in the corollary, and guarantees an improvement over ignoring the outcome only at shorter durations still; both limits shrink when the remainder constant CC grows or when the disturbance moves the outcome less (smaller κ​σ\kappa\sigma), and these constants depend on the system. Whether the transitions of a given system are short enough is therefore an empirical question. Factual data cannot settle it, since the interaction is not identified (); measures it on our simulators.

The first-order argument also extends to certain partially observed inertial systems. With pose-only observations, an unknown initial velocity contributes to the transition, while applied forces affect position at order h2h^{2}. The interaction between the force contribution and the disturbance appears at higher order. Under the conditions of , the mean-squared error of residual reuse is O⁡(h6)O(h^{6}) despite the hidden velocity. If, in addition, distinct disturbances move the pose apart at order h2h^{2}, as in the separation condition of , the variance they induce is at least of order h4h^{4}, and the relative rate is again O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}). This is a specific property of inertial dynamics, rather than a general guarantee for arbitrary insufficient representations.

Minimax optimality.

The short-time bound gives a rate achievable by residual reuse. We next ask whether another estimator could achieve a uniformly smaller risk using the same information. The estimator may know the exact factual transition laws at every action and duration and may condition on the observed factual outcome. It does not observe paired outcomes under different actions for the same disturbance.

Theorem 3.6 (Residual reuse is minimax rate-optimal).

Let ℱC\mathcal{F}_{C} contain every world satisfying the assumptions of , with remainder constant CC for all 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0} and actions in [−1,1][-1,1].

Give an estimator the exact factual transition law at every source, action and duration, together with the observed outcome Yh​(−1)Y_{h}(-1) of a query event at a fixed source. Then, for every 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0},

4​C2​h41+C2​h2\displaystyle\frac{4C^{2}h^{4}}{1+C^{2}h^{2}} ≤infδsupM∈ℱC𝔼M​‖δ−YhM​(1)‖2\displaystyle\leq\inf_{\delta}\sup_{M\in\mathcal{F}_{C}}\mathbb{E}_{M}\bigl\|\delta-Y_{h}^{M}(1)\bigr\|^{2} (26)
≤supM∈ℱC𝔼M​‖TRM−YhM​(1)‖2=4​C2​h4.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{M\in\mathcal{F}_{C}}\mathbb{E}_{M}\bigl\|T_{R}^{M}-Y_{h}^{M}(1)\bigr\|^{2}=4C^{2}h^{4}.

The lower bound already holds within smooth autonomous ODEs with separate action and disturbance channels.

(Proof in .)

The lower and upper bounds agree at leading order as h→0h\to 0. Thus, residual reuse is minimax rate-optimal, with the sharp leading constant, over the stated class of short-time models. The corresponding relative rate is also optimal under the conditions of .

The lower-bound construction uses two worlds with identical factual transition laws but different same-disturbance couplings. The ambiguity is a rotation of the hidden disturbance whose sign cannot be recovered from the factual laws, as in related latent-rotation nonidentification results [37]. The construction is realized by smooth ODEs whose second-order remainder attains the risk bound. It follows that additional model capacity or a more accurate factual likelihood cannot uniformly improve the rate without additional assumptions or information.

This is a worst-case result over ℱC\mathcal{F}_{C}. A known physical mechanism, paired counterfactual observations, or repeated observations of a shared disturbance may permit more accurate estimators for particular systems.

Limits of the short-time approximation.

The expansion () requires the first-order action response to be independent of the disturbance. Three types of violations are relevant.

First, disturbances that directly multiply the command introduce an action–disturbance interaction at first order. For s˙=a​ε\dot{s}=a\varepsilon, the counterfactual error is proportional to h⁡(a−a′)​εh(a-a^{\prime})\varepsilon, and the relative risk can fail to decrease as hh shrinks (). A state-dependent disturbance, such as uncertain damping, is different: it may satisfy the separate-channel ODE model, although the relevant time scale depends on the plant dynamics.

Second, contacts, clipping and actuator saturation can introduce nonsmooth or instantaneous interactions. A transition that crosses a contact boundary can violate the uniform expansion required by the theorem.

Third, the representation can obscure the required structure. Folded coordinates may suppress the first-order disturbance response, while insufficient observations may mix states with different action contrasts. Smoothness of the encoder alone does not resolve state aliasing (). Raw pixels are an extreme case: intensities change sharply at object edges, so the second-order remainder of is very large in pixel coordinates, and a pixel residual does not transport at any duration we test ().

These cases do not contradict the interaction bound: they either increase the interaction, reduce disturbance separation, or violate the assumptions of the short-time expansion. We evaluate them separately in .

The duration hh in these bounds is that of the counterfactual itself, from the action to the observed outcome. Over longer durations, second-order terms can accumulate and the bounds loosen, unless the dynamics settle to an additive equilibrium (); our experiments therefore apply the correction one transition at a time. Reusing an observed residual for later transitions is a different question, which depends on whether the disturbance persists ().

3.4  Reusing Pretrained Encoders and Factual Predictors

The preceding guarantees use the population conditional mean μh\mu_{h}, whereas a counterfactual world model uses the action contrast supplied by a learned predictor. We show that μh\mu_{h} can be learned by ordinary squared-loss training on a frozen pretrained encoder, regardless of its pretraining objective, and that an available factual predictor can be reused when it already supplies the required contrast. We also state when the predicted action contrast equals the conditional average effect of changing the action; by (16), only the error in this contrast contributes additional counterfactual risk.

Squared-loss prediction on frozen representations.

Let ff be a fixed encoder and HtH_{t} the model context already introduced in , a fixed measurable function of observations up to tt and past actions, such as a sequence of frame embeddings and controls. With

Xt=(Ht,𝒂t),Yt=zt+1=f⁡(𝒐t+1),X_{t}=(H_{t},\bm{a}_{t}),\qquad Y_{t}=z_{t+1}=f(\bm{o}_{t+1}),

we retain μ\mu for the population conditional mean and μ^\widehat{\mu} for a fitted predictor, suppressing the fixed transition duration. The encoder can come from any pretraining objective: once ff and the context construction are frozen, squared loss identifies the conditional mean of the next embedding.

Theorem 3.7 (Squared loss identifies the encoded conditional mean).

For fixed measurable context HtH_{t} and encoder ff, assume 𝔼​‖Yt‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|Y_{t}\|^{2}<\infty and let

μ⁡(x)=𝔼⁡[Yt∣Xt=x].\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}\mid X_{t}=x].

Every measurable square-integrable predictor μ^\widehat{\mu} satisfies

𝔼​‖Yt−μ^​(Xt)‖2=𝔼​‖Yt−μ⁡(Xt)‖2+𝔼​‖μ^​(Xt)−μ⁡(Xt)‖2.\mathbb{E}\|Y_{t}-\widehat{\mu}(X_{t})\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\|Y_{t}-\mu(X_{t})\|^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\mu}(X_{t})-\mu(X_{t})\|^{2}. (27)

Hence μ\mu is the unique population squared-loss minimizer up to equality almost surely on the training support, and

𝔼⁡[2​{μ⁡(Xt)−Yt}∣Xt]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[2\{\mu(X_{t})-Y_{t}\}\mid X_{t}\right]=0. (28)

The minimum risk is

minμ^⁡𝔼​‖Yt−μ^​(Xt)‖2=𝔼⁡[tr⁡Var⁡(Yt∣Xt)].\min_{\widehat{\mu}}\mathbb{E}\|Y_{t}-\widehat{\mu}(X_{t})\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(Y_{t}\mid X_{t})\right]. (29)

Moreover, for any measurable positive weight w⁡(Xt)w(X_{t}) satisfying

0<w⁡(Xt)<∞​a.s.,0<𝔼⁡[w⁡(Xt)]<∞,𝔼⁡[w⁡(Xt)​‖Yt‖2]<∞,0<w(X_{t})<\infty\ \text{a.s.},\qquad 0<\mathbb{E}[w(X_{t})]<\infty,\qquad\mathbb{E}[w(X_{t})\|Y_{t}\|^{2}]<\infty,

the set of population minimizers is unchanged:

arg⁡minμ^⁡𝔼⁡[w⁡(Xt)​‖Yt−μ^​(Xt)‖2]={μ^:μ^​(Xt)=μ⁡(Xt)​a.s.}.\arg\min_{\widehat{\mu}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(X_{t})\|Y_{t}-\widehat{\mu}(X_{t})\|^{2}\right]=\{\widehat{\mu}:\widehat{\mu}(X_{t})=\mu(X_{t})\ \text{a.s.}\}. (30)

(Proof in .)

The conditional-expectation decomposition applies to any fixed encoder: pretraining determines the features being predicted, while squared-loss training identifies their conditional mean on the factual support. We can therefore reuse released representations without requiring the original pretraining objective or predictor to match the world-modeling task.

Corollary 3.8 (A released encoder can be reused).

For any frozen encoder checkpoint ff, a predictor trained by squared loss on

(Ht,𝒂t,f⁡(𝒐t+1))\bigl(H_{t},\bm{a}_{t},f(\bm{o}_{t+1})\bigr)

has population target μ\mu. If μ\mu belongs to the predictor class and training attains the minimum population risk, the fitted predictor equals μ\mu almost surely on the training support.

The conclusion is independent of the encoder pretraining objective or the availability of its original predictor, and does not establish representation sufficiency or counterfactual identification.

(Proof in .)

Frozen JEPA encoders, masked autoencoders, contrastively trained representations and supervised checkpoints can thus supply the features for a factual world model. Our experiments fit a new squared-loss predictor on these frozen features; when a pretrained world model already provides the required action contrast for the chosen context and target representation, both its encoder and predictor can instead be reused without retraining. An arbitrary pretrained predictor is not guaranteed to estimate this contrast accurately: its contrast error enters (16), and counterfactual validity still requires supported actions, the identification conditions below and the preceding structural assumptions.

When factual predictions identify action effects.

Squared-loss training identifies μ(Ht,a)=𝔼[Yt∣Ht,At=a]\mu(H_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}\mid H_{t},A_{t}=a], whereas our counterfactual construction requires the interventional contrast 𝔼⁡[Yt​(a′)−Yt​(a)∣Ht]\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}(a^{\prime})-Y_{t}(a)\mid H_{t}]. The difference μ⁡(Ht,a′)−μ⁡(Ht,a)\mu(H_{t},a^{\prime})-\mu(H_{t},a) identifies this contrast under consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity [52, 25]. Conditional exchangeability requires

Yt​(a)⟂⟂At|HtY_{t}(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp A_{t}\mid H_{t}

for each action aa, meaning that the chosen action carries no further information about the potential outcome after conditioning on the model context. This holds when the behavior policy uses only information available to the world model and independent randomization, as formalized below; positivity additionally requires the queried actions to have support at the relevant contexts.

Proposition 3.9 (Shared inputs rule out confounding).

Suppose the behavior policy chooses

𝒂t=πb​(g⁡(Ht),ξt),\bm{a}_{t}=\pi_{b}(g(H_{t}),\xi_{t}),

where gg is measurable and the policy randomization ξt\xi_{t} is conditionally independent of the potential outcomes (Yt​(a))a(Y_{t}(a))_{a} given HtH_{t}.

Then

Yt​(a)⟂⟂𝒂t|HtY_{t}(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp\bm{a}_{t}\mid H_{t}

for every action aa, and, on supported actions,

μ⁡(Ht,a)=𝔼⁡[Yt​(a)∣Ht].\mu(H_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}(a)\mid H_{t}].

(Proof in .)

A controller choosing actions from the observation history supplied to the world model satisfies this condition when its additional randomization is independent of the potential outcomes, even if the physical disturbance is unobserved. If a teleoperator instead adjusts the command using wind information unavailable to the model, the logged action carries additional information about the disturbance and can confound the command effect with the wind effect. Action coverage remains a separate requirement: a deterministic controller may satisfy the shared-input condition while choosing only one action at each context, leaving alternative action contrasts unsupported.

Learning the contrast without propensity weighting.

Under exchangeability and overlap, ordinary squared-loss regression identifies the conditional interventional mean without inverse-propensity weighting: by (), positive input weights leave the unrestricted population minimizer unchanged. This invariance concerns the target, while weighting can affect finite-sample accuracy and the approximation selected by a misspecified predictor class [55]. Propensity-based and doubly robust methods remain useful for other causal targets, including marginal functionals involving nuisance estimation [15], but do not by themselves identify the same-event coupling missing from factual data ().

For counterfactual prediction, the fitted world model only needs to estimate μ⁡(Ht,a′)−μ⁡(Ht,a)\mu(H_{t},a^{\prime})-\mu(H_{t},a) accurately, since errors shared across actions cancel in (16); an action-dependent bias, however, enters the correction directly. Thus, a frozen pretrained encoder and an ordinary factual predictor supply the learned part of our construction whenever their supported action contrast has the required interventional interpretation. The observed outcome supplies the realized residual, and the physical dynamics control how accurately it transfers between actions in the chosen coordinates. We test these requirements below and, separately, test on three large external corpora whether predictors fitted on frozen DINOv2-S and V-JEPA 2 features leave any input-predictable residual ().

Assumptions at a glance.

collects the assumptions of residual reuse, where each is stated formally, and a real system where it holds or fails. The first two make the predicted action contrast causal, the next three keep the action–disturbance interaction small, and the last two concern the coordinates in which the residual is reused. In our benchmarks, the factual action of the evaluated transition is drawn uniformly from the command support, independently of the disturbance, so the first two hold by design; tests the other five.

4  Counterfactual World Models: Empirical Validation

We first test the physical approximation using simulator outcomes, then evaluate counterfactual prediction from pixels with frozen encoders and predictors trained on factual transitions. We examine how the disturbance mechanism and output coordinates affect residual reuse, and conclude with hindsight planning and the effect of disturbance persistence. No counterfactual outcome is used for training or model selection.

4.1  Validating the Physical Approximation

To isolate the interaction error from prediction and readout errors, we evaluate residual reuse in physical coordinates with simulator conditional means estimated by Monte Carlo. For each source state and action pair, we compute

ρ⁡(a,a′)=tr⁡Var⁡(Y⁡(a′)−Y⁡(a))tr⁡Var⁡(Y⁡(a′)).\rho(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}\bigl(Y(a^{\prime})-Y(a)\bigr)}{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(Y(a^{\prime}))}.

By (10), the numerator is the counterfactual risk with exact factual predictions, while the denominator is the minimum risk without the factual outcome. Residual reuse improves on this reference when ρ<1\rho<1.

Interaction determines counterfactual accuracy.

For actuator offsets scored in the directly affected coordinates, ρ≤0.033\rho\leq 0.033 (, left). Small interactions also occur outside additive responses: HandReach fingertip positions and BlueROV2 body velocities have ρ≤0.12\rho\leq 0.12, with ideal residual-reuse R2R^{2} of 94.694.6–98.9%98.9\% against references near 50%50\% without the outcome. Folded pitch coordinates and contact-mediated block velocities instead have ρ>1\rho>1, so residual reuse increases error even with exact factual predictions ().

We also vary the disturbance continuously from an actuator offset to a gain fault,

σ​ε​[(1−λ)+λ​aamax],λ∈[0,1],\sigma\varepsilon\left[(1-\lambda)+\lambda\frac{a}{a_{\max}}\right],\qquad\lambda\in[0,1],

while calibrating the physical parameters before evaluation to keep the reference without the outcome near 50%50\% R2R^{2}. The equilibrium model predicts ρ=0\rho=0, 0.50.5 and 22 at λ=0\lambda=0, 0.50.5 and 11 (derivation in ). HandReach and Ball-in-Cup follow this prediction: at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5, their measured ratios are 0.500.50 and 0.480.48; at λ=1\lambda=1, they are 2.012.01 and 1.971.97 (, right). The error therefore follows the action–disturbance interaction as the disturbance changes from additive to multiplicative.

Short transitions and additive equilibria.

The short-time result predicts ρh=O⁡(h2)\rho_{h}=O(h^{2}) under separate smooth action and disturbance channels. On a damped pendulum, an uncertain damping coefficient gives the predicted h2h^{2} dependence, whereas an additive force gives the faster h8h^{8} decrease (, left). Gain faults and actuator saturation instead maintain ratios near 2.062.06 and 0.060.06 over the tested durations. These mechanisms distinguish a small interaction from one that decreases as the transition becomes shorter.

Native position servos provide a second route to approximate additivity. In HandReach, the offset interaction ratio decreases from 0.190.19 at 0.04​s0.04\,\mathrm{s} to 0.00080.0008 at 0.32​s0.32\,\mathrm{s} as the actuators settle to an approximately additive setpoint; fingertip coordinates settle near ρ=0.07\rho=0.07, while gain faults remain near 22 (, right). This improvement at longer durations comes from the equilibrium response. It is distinct from the short-time guarantee and shows why the dynamics, duration and measured coordinates must be considered together.

4.2  Counterfactual Prediction from Pixels

Environments and factual training.

We use seven native simulators rendered at 224×224224\times 224: HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach, liquid transport (PassWater), Racetrack, Push-T and BlueROV2 (). Each transition receives a bounded disturbance with a physical meaning, such as an offset in a servo target, force, position goal or thrust. After two transitions of a task-directed behavior policy, we sample a factual action and three distinct alternative actions uniformly from the declared command support. Evaluation branches share the same source state and realized disturbance. We calibrate the environments so that both actions and disturbances affect the outcome and verify image-based recovery of the scored quantities; the complete design and observability protocol is in and . The primary comparisons use HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach, PassWater and BlueROV2; Racetrack and Push-T are retained as diagnostics.

Images are encoded by frozen, publicly released self-supervised vision transformers, without fine-tuning: DINOv2 [40], trained by self-distillation, in its small and base sizes (DINOv2-S, DINOv2-B), and the masked autoencoder MAE [23], trained to reconstruct masked image patches, in its base size (MAE-B). These two cover the two main families of self-supervised pretraining, joint embedding and reconstruction, and DINOv2 is the encoder of recent JEPA world models [64]. Each frame is represented by the encoder’s class-token (CLS) embedding. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3-B [56], SigLIP 2-B [58], CLIP-B [50] and EVA-02-B [16], go through the same pipeline, each with the default pooling of its released checkpoint ( and ). A predictor with two attention blocks of width 1,0241{,}024 receives k∈{1,2,3}k\in\{1,2,3\} frame embeddings, past actions and the query action. It is fitted on all recorded factual transitions using

ℒfactual=𝔼train​‖dθ​(Ht(k),at)−zt+1−ztr‖2,μ^k​(H,a)=zt+r​dθ​(H,a),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{factual}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{train}}\Bigl\|d_{\theta}(H_{t}^{(k)},a_{t})-\frac{z_{t+1}-z_{t}}{r}\Bigr\|^{2},\qquad\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H,a)=z_{t}+r\,d_{\theta}(H,a), (31)

where rr scales feature displacements using fitting data only. Architecture, regularization and checkpoints are selected by held-out factual error (). The counterfactual prediction is

z^t+1CF=zt+1+μ^k​(Ht(k),a′)−μ^k​(Ht(k),at).\widehat{z}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{CF}}=z_{t+1}+\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H_{t}^{(k)},a^{\prime})-\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H_{t}^{(k)},a_{t}). (32)

Residual correction adds no parameters or training stage. Each world model is thus a JEPA: it predicts the next embedding, never pixels, including with MAE-B, whose pretraining reconstructs pixels. Encoder specifications are in .

Evaluation and baselines.

Frozen nonlinear readouts π\pi are fitted on factual frames with physical-state targets. They provide physical units for evaluation and coordinates in which we can apply residual correction directly, as in (); we compare this construction with decoding the corrected embedding. No counterfactual label enters fitting or model selection. We report physical counterfactual R2R^{2} on prespecified coordinates: one minus the squared error of the predicted coordinates, summed over coordinates and queries, divided by the summed variance of their true counterfactual values. Intervals are bootstrapped over source states and training seeds.

The trained predictor, π⁡(μ^k​(H,a′))\pi(\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H,a^{\prime})), shares all weights with the counterfactual model but does not observe the factual outcome. The oracle predictor (no outcome) knows the full simulator source state and averages the true dynamics over the disturbance law, giving the optimal squared-error prediction with that information. Factual copying, π⁡(zt+1)\pi(z_{t+1}), tests whether the alternative action matters, while shuffling factual outcomes across disturbance draws tests whether the correction uses information specific to the observed event.

Counterfactual accuracy.

With one frame and 88k factual episodes per environment, correction after the readout reaches 85.685.6–95.7%95.7\% R2R^{2} on HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and PassWater, compared with 38.138.1–45.6%45.6\% for the same trained predictors and 49.149.1–51.1%51.1\% for the oracle predictors without the outcome (). Factual copying reaches 6.76.7–43.5%43.5\%, and shuffling outcomes reduces counterfactual accuracy to between −14.6-14.6 and 6.3%6.3\% (). Thus, the improvement uses the realized disturbance information in the factual outcome; it cannot be explained by copying that outcome or improving the underlying predictor. The four further encoders give the same picture: on the same four environments, wherever they pass our disturbance-recovery criterion, correction after the readout reaches 81.081.0–95.3%95.3\%, against 34.734.7–45.4%45.4\% for their trained predictors, and DINOv3-B gives the highest values of all seven encoders on HandReach and Ball-in-Cup, 88.888.8 and 95.0%95.0\% ().

The interaction ratios of and  are computed from simulator outcomes in physical coordinates, so they are the same for every encoder. An encoder changes the counterfactual error only through the error of the learned action contrast, the second term of (16), and through the readout: across the seven encoders, correction after the readout ranges over 81.081.0–88.8%88.8\% on HandReach, against 98.3%98.3\% with exact simulator means.

BlueROV2 requires more factual data. With the same 88k episodes, correction after the readout reaches 70.770.7–74.2%74.2\% with MAE-B and DINOv2, and 75.5%75.5\% with DINOv3-B, against 51.8%51.8\% for the oracle predictor without the outcome. Correction in feature space reaches only 46.146.1–53.0%53.0\%. The complete comparison, including seed ensembles, larger data budgets and the diagnostic Push-T results, is in .

Correction without state labels.

The two constructions of need different supervision. Correction in feature space, (), uses only the frozen encoder and the factual predictor, so it applies to any pretrained representation. Correction after the readout, (), also needs the readout, fitted on physical-state labels of factual frames. We score both through the same readout, which any evaluation in physical units requires. Without labels, correction in feature space reaches 73.473.4–94.1%94.1\% on HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and PassWater, against 38.138.1–45.6%45.6\% for the trained predictors, so most of the gain needs no state supervision. The readout adds 1.41.4–4.34.3 points on the first three and 12.112.1–17.717.7 points on PassWater. On BlueROV2, the readout is needed: correction in feature space stays near the oracle predictor without the outcome at the standard data size, and reaches 65.965.9–72.2%72.2\% with sixteen times the data, against 90.190.1–93.5%93.5\% after the readout (). traces this gap to the coordinates: the full feature vector is not additive, and the readout selects coordinates in which the action and the disturbance nearly add.

Factual predictor quality.

Equation (16) separates the interaction error from the error in the predicted action contrast. Selecting the predictor configuration by factual validation loss reduces factual error by 88–17%17\% in every tested cell and improves or preserves counterfactual accuracy in five of six environments (). Push-T provides an exception: factual feature error improves while the predicted pusher action contrast becomes less accurate. Factual loss over the full feature vector therefore provides an imperfect measure of the action contrast required by residual reuse.

Increasing the factual data improves counterfactual prediction without changing the correction. With MAE-B, an eightfold increase raises readout-corrected R2R^{2} from 69.869.8 to 85.6%85.6\% on HandReach, 80.880.8 to 94.2%94.2\% on Ball-in-Cup, 90.790.7 to 95.7%95.7\% on FetchReach and 83.983.9 to 94.8%94.8\% on PassWater (). BlueROV2 reaches 85.785.7–88.2%88.2\% across encoders with four times the standard data and 90.190.1–93.5%93.5\% with sixteen times the data; its oracle predictor without the outcome remains at 51.8%51.8\%. These results identify factual prediction error as a practical limitation even when the physical interaction is small.

Observation history.

In this ablation, each disturbance has two components (): a fresh one, independent and identically distributed (IID) over transitions, and a persistent one, correlated across transitions. Past frames can reveal the persistent component, whereas only the current outcome carries information about the fresh one. The main benchmark is fully fresh. On HandReach, increasing the fresh share of disturbance variance from 2525 to 100%100\% reduces the trained predictor’s R2R^{2} from 71.771.7 to 38.1%38.1\%, whereas the counterfactual model goes only from 91.491.4 to 85.6%85.6\% (). With half the variance persistent, increasing the context from one to three frames changes trained-predictor accuracy by −2.3-2.3 to +2.1+2.1 points and counterfactual accuracy by −4.5-4.5 to +1.6+1.6 points. The population benefit of additional history is therefore not consistently realized by these finite fitted models. The formal risk comparison and complete history results are given in and .

4.3  Conditions and Limits of Residual Reuse

The interaction analysis predicts how residual reuse changes with the measured coordinates and the disturbance mechanism. We test both using the same factual-training procedure, with a separate factual predictor fitted for each disturbance condition.
