Nonlinear responses and external forces.

The HandReach predictor also produces accurate fingertip counterfactuals through a second readout fitted on factual frames. On the seven prespecified fingertip coordinates, MAE-B reaches 83.6%83.6\% R2R^{2} with correction in feature space, against 39.8%39.8\% for the trained predictor, −1.3%-1.3\% for factual copying and 53.0%53.0\% for the oracle predictor without the outcome. The simulator reference with exact means reaches 96.5%96.5\% (). These nonlinear coordinates therefore retain much of the benefit found on the directly actuated wrist.

Residual reuse also works when the disturbance acts on the plant rather than through the command. An external load applied at the HandReach palm reaches the wrist through the configuration-dependent force Jacobian. Its measured interaction is small, ρ≤0.001\rho\leq 0.001, and the learned counterfactual reaches 88.7%88.7\% with MAE-B and 86.9%86.9\% with DINOv2-S after the readout, against 3939–40%40\% for the trained predictors and 50%50\% for the oracle predictor without the outcome (). The disturbance’s point of entry therefore does not determine whether correction succeeds; its interaction with the action does.

Output coordinates.

The same physics can give different interaction errors in different coordinates. For BlueROV2, sin⁡(pitch)\sin(\mathrm{pitch}) is additive with ρ=0\rho=0, whereas the folded coordinate cos⁡(pitch)\cos(\mathrm{pitch}) gives ρ=1.67\rho=1.67. For the actuator-offset conditions, applying correction after the physical readout improves on decoding the corrected embedding in every environment, by 1.41.4 to 25.925.9 points (, including diagnostic Push-T). The readout thus supplies both physical quantities and coordinates with smaller action–disturbance interactions; accurate physical counterfactuals do not establish additivity of the full feature vector ( gives an explicit example).

Currents that vary in space and time.

A uniform current makes residual reuse exact on the title-page boat, so one may ask how constant the disturbance must be. We vary the eddies of its current along two axes, with their speed and the mean flow fixed: their size, through the shortest wavelength LL from 10001000 boat lengths down to 1.251.25, and how fast their pattern drifts in time, from 00 to 33 radians per transition. Each condition has its own 128128k factual episodes, frozen MAE-B readout and factual predictor (). In space, the interaction ratio grows as 1/L21/L^{2}, from 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} at L=1000L=1000 to 0.080.08 at L=5L=5: the gradient of the current scales as 1/L1/L, and it sets how differently the current pushes the boat at the endpoints of two headings, one boat length apart. The growth slows once the waves approach the length of the move, and ρ\rho reaches 0.490.49 at L=1.25L=1.25. The counterfactual world model follows ρ\rho with a nearly constant estimation error: its relative risk lies 0.120.12 to 0.150.15 above ρ\rho at every size, from 0.130.13 to 0.640.64, while the trained predictor stays at 1.111.11–1.171.17, slightly above the oracle predictor without the outcome (). In time, ρ\rho stays at 0.0200.020–0.0220.022 and the counterfactual relative risk at 0.150.15–0.170.17 for every phase rate: all headings of an event meet the field at the same instants, so the correction depends on how the current differs between the places the actions lead to, not on how it changes over time. A change over time would matter only if a residual observed in one transition were reused in a later one. Residual reuse therefore needs a disturbance that varies little over the distance separating the outcomes of alternative actions. These collections are diagnostic, since the oracle predictor already reaches 8686–97%97\% position R2R^{2} and recovery of the north-south drift falls just below 95%95\% ().

Pixels do not transport.

Residual reuse needs coordinates in which actions and disturbances add, and raw pixels lack them even with exact means. On the title-page boat () with a uniform current, for which correction after the readout is exact, we transport the observed outcome with Monte Carlo conditional means over the current, so no model is fitted and only the coordinates change. In pixels, the interaction ratio is 2.132.13: the current displaces the boat’s edges, which lie elsewhere under the alternative heading, so adding the difference of mean images leaves a dark imprint and a blurred copy rather than a displaced boat. Read back through the frozen encoder and readout, these images give a relative risk of 5.865.86 against the true position, far worse than ignoring the outcome. The 768768 MAE-B features are not additive in their own metric either (ρ=1.92\rho=1.92), yet correction in feature space still carries the displacement into the readout (relative risk 0.310.31), and correction after the readout reaches 0.0020.002. Shorter transitions do not rescue pixels: their ratio stays between 1.741.74 and 2.182.18 from h=1h=1 to h=0.05h=0.05 (). Pixel intensities change sharply at the boat’s edges, so the second-order term of becomes small only for moves well below a pixel, and even at h=0.05h=0.05 the commanded move spans about 1.41.4 pixels. Counterfactual world models therefore reuse residuals in compact coordinates read out from a learned representation; a world model that predicts pixels would need such coordinates before its residual could be reused.

Contacts and multiplicative faults.

Push-T block velocities depend on whether the disturbed command produces contact. Their interaction ratios exceed one, and residual reuse with exact simulator means gives R2R^{2} values of 5.65.6, −15.5-15.5 and −44.4%-44.4\%, below the references without the outcome at 2020–39%39\% (). The failure is present before fitting a visual predictor.

The learned gain-fault experiment follows the interaction increase found in . At λ=0.5\lambda=0.5, correction in feature space reaches 70.570.5–70.6%70.6\%, above the oracle predictor without the outcome at 52.9%52.9\%. At λ=1\lambda=1, it falls to 6.46.4–11.0%11.0\%, below the trained predictors at 4141–42%42\%; correction after the readout falls further, to between −12.8-12.8 and −11.8%-11.8\% ( and ). These λ>0\lambda>0 cells are diagnostic, since disturbance recovery from the frozen features falls below 95%95\%. A more accurate factual predictor cannot remove the interaction responsible for the exact-mean residual error. Complete physical checks, observability results and the uncertain-damping experiments are in and .

4.4  Planning with the Observed Outcome

Hindsight planning asks which command would have reached a goal in the event that just occurred, e.g., which heading would have brought the boat of to a mooring under the current it met. A retry, the correction of later commands under a persistent fault and the diagnosis of a failed attempt all need this answer; we test the first two below. We evaluate whether improved counterfactual predictions change the action selected for an observed event. After one factual transition, the planner receives a goal reached by another action under the same source state and disturbance. It selects a command, which we score by replaying that event. The goal is attainable by construction. The trained predictor and counterfactual model share the same frozen models, those of except on BlueROV2, which uses its 3232k-episode predictors; the oracle planners use the true simulator, either averaging over the disturbance law or observing the realized disturbance. All planners use the same cross-entropy search, except that on liquid transport the true-simulator planners use 1616 candidates per round (). Success requires standardized distance to the goal below 0.20.2; full protocols are in .

The counterfactual world model succeeds in 3535–69%69\% of events, compared with 99–25%25\% for the trained predictor and 1414–23%23\% for the oracle planner without the outcome (). Its gain over the latter is positive in all ten environment–encoder comparisons, with bootstrap intervals above zero. The oracle planner observing the true disturbance succeeds in every event (). Thus, the observed outcome supplies information useful for action selection even when the comparison planner knows the true dynamics. The oracle without the outcome minimizes expected squared distance; it is a reference for that objective, not a universal upper bound on thresholded success.

Repeated attempts and subsequent transitions.

Two additional attempts on the same event raise counterfactual-model success to 5151–97%97\%, while the trained predictor remains at 99–24%24\%. Over three consecutive transitions, a persistent fault, one disturbance held for the whole episode, gives an improvement from 44–25%25\% to 1111–51%51\%, whereas fresh disturbances, redrawn independently at every transition, give changes of only −4-4 to 66 points. Without disturbances, residual correction reduces replanning success by 44–1515 points, although it still improves same-event retries by 1313–5858 points ( and ). The command-specific prediction-error analysis in explains this dependence: the observed residual predicts the error for the same event and for later transitions under a persistent fault, but not for later independent disturbances. The planning benefit therefore depends on whether the disturbance revealed by the outcome also affects the action being evaluated.

5  Conclusion

We proposed counterfactual world models, which give world models a capability that factual training cannot provide on its own, at the cost of two predictor calls and one addition. The argument has one thread: individual counterfactuals cannot be learned from unpaired data, physics supplies the missing structure when disturbances enter through their own channel, that structure dictates residual reuse, no estimator using unpaired data can uniformly improve its rate, and the experiments confirm both its successes and its failures. The rule is valid where the action–disturbance interaction is small in the chosen representation, which physics provides for force-like disturbances over short transitions and for servoed setpoints once they settle: natura non facit saltus. Where nature leaps, as through contacts, or where the disturbance scales the command instead of adding its own force, the recipe fails, measurably.

The residual carries the event, the world model carries the action. On the boat of , the residual between the observed and predicted positions is the drift caused by the current in this event; in HandReach, it is the wrist offset produced by the miscalibrated servo; in BlueROV2, the pitch change produced by the thruster offset. The world model supplies only how far the change of command moves the system. Our benchmarks are calibrated so that the disturbance carries about half of the counterfactual variance, which no predictor that ignores the outcome can explain (oracle near 50%50\%); on HandReach, the same predictor explains 38.1%38.1\% without the residual and 85.6%85.6\% with it (). The remaining error has two sources, as in (16): the interaction, which no predictor can remove, and the error of the learned action contrast, to which the readout adds its own. With exact simulator means, residual reuse explains 98.398.3–100%100\% of the counterfactual variance on the primary coordinates of HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, BlueROV2 and the Push-T pusher ( and ). On these coordinates, most of the gap between the learned and the ideal counterfactual therefore comes from learning, consistent with the gains from more factual data ().

The operating window is set by the interaction, not by the clock. The interaction ratio is the quantity to check. With exact factual predictions, residual reuse beats the best predictor that ignores the outcome exactly when this ratio is below one, which guarantees when the interaction, scaled by the size of the action change, is small compared with how strongly the disturbance moves the outcome. In our simulators, the ratio stays well below one over one transition for every offset and external load of and , in coordinates without folds or contacts, and it even decreases at longer durations once servos settle (). Gain faults keep it near two at every tested duration, and contacts push it above one. Damping faults show where the window closes for a disturbance that does enter through its own channel: they move the outcome so little over these durations that their ratio stays at 0.740.74–1.081.08 (); for such weak disturbances, guarantees a ratio below one only over durations proportional to κ​σ\kappa\sigma, a window that narrows with the disturbance. The ratio itself needs paired outcomes, so it is an evaluation diagnostic, not a quantity one can compute from factual logs before deployment. Factual data can flag a large interaction, such as a gain fault, which spreads the outcome more under larger commands, but cannot certify a small one (); certifying a small interaction on a new system needs another source: knowledge of where the disturbance enters, a simulator, or paired trials under a disturbance that persists long enough to try two actions.

We now draw one consequence for each of the three fields this work connects: world models, causal inference and control.

For world models, a factual world model already contains a counterfactual one. It takes two queries of the same predictor and the observed outcome. Its accuracy is bounded by physics and approached by the factual world model: with sixteen times more factual data, the same recipe moves the BlueROV2 underwater vehicle from 73.673.6 to 93.5%93.5\% (94.1%94.1\% with seed ensembles), while the trained predictor stays below the oracle predictor (no outcome). Accurate counterfactuals need no paired data, latent disturbance model or extra training, but they do need the observed outcome, coordinates in which the response is near-additive, and features that determine the action response. Generative likelihood, however good, does not supply the missing coupling ().

For causal inference, mechanics turns an identification assumption into a physical one. For physical systems, the additive noise assumption that identifies counterfactuals holds approximately when the action and the disturbance enter through separate channels, with an explicit approximation rate and explicit failure modes. The assumption concerns physical coordinates, such as those read out from learned image features, and need not hold in the features themselves: on the boat, MAE-B features give ρ=1.92\rho=1.92 (). The interaction ratio is a scale-free diagnostic of how far a system is from the additive noise model in given coordinates (), measurable in simulation or from paired trials, but not from factual logs alone.

For control, classical disturbance estimators extend to learned image world models. Disturbance observers, offset-free model predictive control and iterative learning control are counterfactual estimators, usually analyzed with a known nominal model, often a linear or linearized one [13, 41, 11]. Our analysis extends their reasoning to nonlinear models learned on frozen image features, at the price of an interaction term that is second order for force-like disturbances and first order for multiplicative faults. In planning, the same construction lets a frozen image world model (i) choose in hindsight better than the true simulator without the outcome, (ii) correct a retried event, as iterative learning control does, and (iii) reject a persistent fault, as offset-free control does; when nothing persists, the transported residual is independent of the next error and costs success ().

Limitations. Residual reuse inherits four limits from its derivation. First, it needs coordinates in which the effects of the action and the disturbance add. A physical readout can provide them where raw pixels do not, and even a readout fails where it folds, as cos⁡(pitch)\cos(\mathrm{pitch}) does (); a world model without a compact readout must first find such coordinates. Fitting the readout needs physical-state labels on factual frames; without them, correction in feature space keeps most of the gain on four environments and about half of it on BlueROV2 (). Second, it needs the disturbance to enter through its own channel, the transition to avoid contacts, and the duration to keep the interaction small; the failures of require the additional information listed in . Third, it reuses one observed residual over one transition. It does not chain counterfactuals over long horizons, and the residual helps later decisions only when the disturbance persists (). Fourth, the predicted contrast must be causal: we assume that the logged actions depended on nothing the world model does not see (), and leave logs from operators who perceived more than was recorded for future work.

Scope of the evidence. All environments are simulated, and their disturbances are controlled actuator faults with stated physical meaning, not exhaustive models of real-world uncertainty. Our scores concern prespecified physical coordinates decoded from frozen frame embeddings, not full simulator state or Markov sufficiency. The planning tasks use one-transition search, at most three steps and goals in those coordinates, and the one-shot and retry tasks score a hindsight decision by replaying the event in simulation. Two of seven environments fail our criteria for recovering the scored quantities or the disturbance from images (); BlueROV2 passes only with a four times larger factual collection for its disturbance readout. The oracle references of HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and BlueROV2 are Monte Carlo estimates that agree with independent numerical refinements but carry no formal numerical-error bound, and PassWater’s uses only four disturbance draws per source state ().

Open directions. Each limit suggests a direction. (i) The paired trials above could tell, before deployment, where residual reuse is safe on a real system. (ii) Since the error is set by the interaction in the chosen coordinates, an encoder or readout could be trained, in simulation or from such trials, so that actions and disturbances add, turning additivity from a property we check into one we learn. (iii) Contacts and gain faults call for transport rules that switch with the contact mode or rescale the residual with the command, combining residual reuse with the other structures of . (iv) Factual error over the whole feature vector is an imperfect proxy for the action contrast: selecting the factual predictor by held-out error improves or preserves the counterfactual in five of six environments but not on Push-T, and a criterion targeted at the action response could close part of the gap left by learning. (v) Chaining counterfactuals over several transitions, each with its own observed outcome, would extend the uses that motivated counterfactual reasoning in reinforcement learning, such as credit assignment, data augmentation and explanation [33, 47, 60], to learned world models of physical systems. Finally, the argument never uses that the system is a robot: any process with smooth dynamics and a hidden perturbation that enters through its own channel admits the same answer after a surprise. We hope this study makes the observed outcome a first-class input of world models, as offset-free control has long made it for its own models.

Appendix A Tables for the Main-Text Figures

All R2R^{2} values are percentages. CF WM denotes counterfactual world model.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocol

Qualification.

Each condition fixes the physics, query population, scored coordinates and readouts before fitting. Qualification requires held-out disturbance and retained-coordinate recovery of at least 95%95\%, and oracle (no outcome) and factual-outcome-copy R2R^{2} strictly below 60%60\% on the same population; simulation also checks true-state factual copying. A condition is qualified only when every criterion has been measured and passes; an unmeasured criterion leaves it unqualified. We call each criterion a gate; conditions that fail a gate are reported as diagnostics. Recovery is checked on held-out factual episodes and on an independent confirmation cohort of new source states collected after the physical setting was selected. A parent is a source state from which the factual and all query branches are simulated with the same disturbance draw; the scored source is the t=2t=2 anchor, reached after two behavior-policy transitions. The numerical checks of the physical references are reported separately in ().

B.1  No-Outcome Information Sets

Let Ht(k)=(zt−k+1,at−k+1,…,at−1,zt)H_{t}^{(k)}=(z_{t-k+1},a_{t-k+1},\ldots,a_{t-1},z_{t}) denote a causal kk-frame observation history. Past commands are included, the current command is replaced by the query a′a^{\prime}, and the current endpoint zt+1z_{t+1} is absent. Write Y=St+1⋆​(a′)Y=S_{t+1}^{\star}(a^{\prime}) for the retained physical counterfactual coordinates and Ik=(Ht(k),a′)I_{k}=(H_{t}^{(k)},a^{\prime}). The ideal no-outcome predictor, the oracle (no outcome) given IkI_{k}, and its risk are

bk∗​(Ik)\displaystyle b_{k}^{*}(I_{k}) =𝔼⁡[Y∣Ik],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid I_{k}], (33)
RBayes,k2\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{Bayes},k}^{2} =1−𝔼​tr⁡Var​(Y∣Ik)𝔼​‖Y−𝔼​Y‖2.\displaystyle=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid I_{k})}{\mathbb{E}\|Y-\mathbb{E}Y\|^{2}}. (34)

This is a population squared-error ceiling for predictors with information IkI_{k}; it is neither a ceiling for a predictor that observes the current factual endpoint nor a universal constant independent of history or population. The fully fresh simulator reference used in the main text conditions on the full physical source and query action, a stronger information set than a single image, and estimates conditional noise variance from independent same-source simulator branches. All branching is evaluation-only; the plotted reference includes Monte Carlo uncertainty.

The practical baseline is a fitted embedding predictor,

z^t+1det=μ^k​(Ht(k),a′),Y^det=π⁡(z^t+1det),\widehat{z}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{det}}=\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H_{t}^{(k)},a^{\prime}),\qquad\widehat{Y}_{\mathrm{det}}=\pi(\widehat{z}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{det}}), (35)

where π\pi is the frozen nonlinear physical readout. Factual squared loss has the population target 𝔼[zt+1∣Ht(k),At=a]\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid H_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}=a], which sufficient data, capacity and successful optimization can approximate. They do not generally make π⁡(𝔼⁡[zt+1∣Ik])\pi(\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid I_{k}]) equal 𝔼⁡[π⁡(zt+1)∣Ik]\mathbb{E}[\pi(z_{t+1})\mid I_{k}], and cannot supply physical variables absent from the observation. The practical decoded predictor need not reach the physical oracle even in an idealized infinite-data limit, so the oracle and learned bars must remain separate.

History and counterfactual risk.

Proposition B.1 (History helps prediction; exact additive cancellation is already complete).

On a fixed population, let ℐ1⊆ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{2} be nested no-current-outcome information sets. Their optimal squared risks satisfy

ℛ1∗−ℛ2∗=𝔼​‖𝔼⁡[Y∣ℐ2]−𝔼⁡[Y∣ℐ1]‖2≥0.\mathcal{R}_{1}^{*}-\mathcal{R}_{2}^{*}=\mathbb{E}\|\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{I}_{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{I}_{1}]\|^{2}\geq 0. (36)

If the factual means identify the potential-outcome means given each history, the population residual risk is ℛR,k=𝔼​tr⁡Var⁡(Δ∣H(k))\mathcal{R}_{R,k}=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\mid H^{(k)}) and decreases under nested histories by 𝔼​‖𝔼⁡[Δ∣H(2)]−𝔼⁡[Δ∣H(1)]‖2\mathbb{E}\|\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid H^{(2)}]-\mathbb{E}[\Delta\mid H^{(1)}]\|^{2}. If the action contrast is determined by the shorter history, both residual risks are zero: history has no error left to remove. (Proof in .)

Persistent disturbances.

For the Gaussian driver in , write gt=1−α​bt+α​ηtg_{t}=\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,b_{t}+\sqrt{\alpha}\,\eta_{t} with bt=b​(t/ℓ)⊤​ξb_{t}=b(t/\ell)^{\top}\xi and a unit-variance IID innovation ηt\eta_{t} independent of pre-transition information. Then

Var⁡(gt∣Ht(k))=(1−α)​Var⁡(bt∣Ht(k))+α.\operatorname{Var}(g_{t}\mid H_{t}^{(k)})=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Var}(b_{t}\mid H_{t}^{(k)})+\alpha. (37)

This identity concerns driver variance, not physical prediction error after nonlinear dynamics. Even at α=1\alpha=1, history may help recover hidden state. The smooth-noise Monte Carlo reference conditions on the native reset, past commands and realized past drivers, and integrates the current driver under its conditional Gaussian law. It excludes the current outcome and driver. Its privileged past contains each compared image window, making its R2R^{2} an upper bound on the image-window optimum, so a value above 60%60\% does not by itself show that the best image-history predictor exceeds that threshold. A frozen image predictor provides a lower bound for its actual information set. Pointwise bounds are not combined into a joint confidence interval.

B.2  Encoder Specifications

The counterfactual experiments use frozen DINOv2-S and DINOv2-B [40] and MAE-B [23], retaining their CLS tokens (384, 768 and 768 coordinates, respectively). All receive bilinearly resized full-frame 224×224224\times 224 images, without center cropping, followed by ImageNet channel normalization. This explicitly overrides the DINOv2 checkpoint’s default input size. No physical coordinate is concatenated with the features. The encoder comparison of adds DINOv3-B, SigLIP 2-B, CLIP-B (trained on LAION-2B) and EVA-02-B, through the timm checkpoints vit_base_patch16_dinov3.lvd1689m, vit_base_patch16_siglip_224.v2_webli, vit_base_patch16_clip_224.laion2b and eva02_base_patch14_224.mim_in22k, each with 768 coordinates: the mean patch token for DINOv3-B, EVA-02-B and SigLIP 2-B, whose attention-pooling head is not used, and the CLS token for CLIP-B. They receive the same resized frames, each with its own channel normalization. The code release records model identifiers, checkpoint hashes, normalization and pooling, and checks them at extraction and inference.

Feature displacement is scaled by

r=max⁡{10−4,[dz−1​∑jVar^fit​(zt+1,j−zt,j)]1/2}.r=\max\left\{10^{-4},\left[d_{z}^{-1}\sum_{j}\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\rm fit}(z_{t+1,j}-z_{t,j})\right]^{1/2}\right\}.

Conditioning means and standard deviations use fitting episodes only, with a 10−410^{-4} standard-deviation floor. A scalar output scale preserves the relative feature weights in the squared loss. Predictions are returned to the original feature coordinates before decoding or residual correction.

B.3  Factual Fitting and Evaluation

There are 8,192 independent factual episodes per environment, each with three transitions. Whole-episode splitting gives 6,553 fitting, 820 validation and 819 reserved episodes per seed. The selected recipe uses all recorded fitting transitions, two width-1,024 attention blocks, four heads per block and multilayer perceptron (MLP) ratio one. History lengths k=1,2,3k=1,2,3 share capacity and initialization policy. Fits use seeds 0,1,20,1,2, 20,000 updates, batch size 256, AdamW learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 0.30.3 and cosine scheduling. Checkpoints minimize factual validation loss at the t=2t=2 anchor, checked every 100 updates. The selection grid is specified in . No counterfactual outcome selects a seed, encoder or checkpoint.

Frozen DINOv2-S, DINOv2-B and MAE-B encode each frame separately (); the predictor receives no physical-state labels. The state and disturbance heads have three hidden layers of width 1,024, 30,000 updates, AdamW learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and factual-validation checkpoint selection. Physical labels supervise these evaluation heads only.

The predictor outputs a normalized feature displacement dθd_{\theta} and minimizes the factual loss of (),

ℒfactual=𝔼train​‖dθ​(Ht(k),at)−zt+1−ztr‖2,μ^k​(H,a)=zt+r​dθ​(H,a),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{factual}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{train}}\left\|d_{\theta}(H_{t}^{(k)},a_{t})-\frac{z_{t+1}-z_{t}}{r}\right\|^{2},\qquad\widehat{\mu}_{k}(H,a)=z_{t}+r\,d_{\theta}(H,a), (38)

where rr is the fitting-only root mean square of the feature-displacement standard deviations; input state/action standardization is also fitted only on training episodes. This differs from physical-state supervision by a frozen head: no physical target is used in this loss. Residual inference adds the observed endpoint to the difference of two queries of the same fitted predictor, as in (), and requires no second training stage. Both arms therefore share the encoder, predictor weights, factual training budget and checkpoint: residual reuse changes only inference and adds no learned parameters. Same-disturbance alternative outcomes enter exclusively in evaluation; the supervised diagnostic heads neither train nor select the factual predictor. All training, validation and checkpoint selection use the stable-pretraining library.

Coordinates and recovery.

The masks are two wrist angles (HandReach), cup x,zx,z (Ball-in-Cup), end-effector x,y,zx,y,z (FetchReach), heading and lane offset (Racetrack), sin⁡(pitch)\sin(\mathrm{pitch}) (BlueROV2), glass xx (PassWater), and pusher x,yx,y (Push-T). These are selected actuator or pose coordinates, not full task state: they do not establish finger, ball, fluid-particle or block-contact counterfactual accuracy. Every retained coordinate must exceed the image recovery threshold; no coordinate is dropped after inspecting CF performance. HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach, PassWater and BlueROV2 (with the disturbance readout of ) pass both held-factual and confirmation image gates with all three encoders. With DINOv2-B on HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and PassWater, disturbance recovery is 96.096.0–98.3%98.3\% held-out and 96.496.4–98.4%98.4\% on confirmation, state recovery 98.698.6–99.9%99.9\% and 98.498.4–99.8%99.8\%, and the upper 95%95\% bounds of the oracle predictor (no outcome) and factual copying are at most 55.555.5 and 53.2%53.2\%. Racetrack fails heading and disturbance recovery; Push-T fails disturbance recovery. A failed fitted recovery head does not prove that the representation contains no such information. State heads read one frame, while the shared disturbance head reads (zt,at,zt+1)(z_{t},a_{t},z_{t+1}) at every history length; its failure blocks the common-screen comparison but does not establish that a separately fitted history-aware disturbance head would also fail. Disturbance recovery is a conservative benchmark eligibility requirement, not a necessary condition of the residual-cancellation theorem.

Numerical checks and uncertainty.

PassWater’s native confirmation has only 128 parents with four disturbance draws each, below the declared minimum of 64 draws; its intervals are therefore especially limited. The other scored native cohorts use 128 parents ×\times 128 draws (HandReach), 512 ×\times 128 (Ball-in-Cup), and 256 ×\times 128 (FetchReach), with three unequal query actions per parent. All rows and all predeclared seeds are retained. The shuffle control of replaces the observed outcome by that of another disturbance draw of the same parent before applying the correction. Reported aggregate physical R2R^{2} uses the summed squared errors and summed target variances of the fixed coordinates. Pointwise intervals use 512 paired whole-parent and fitting-seed bootstrap draws; the point estimate is average single-fit risk, not the risk of an ensemble. These intervals condition on the fixed readouts and collected training data; three fitting seeds do not characterize every source of pipeline variability. The oracle predictor (no outcome) is a Monte Carlo reference conditioned on the full current simulator state and query action, without the current outcome or disturbance; fresh disturbances make its conditional law independent of the past. It uses more information than the image predictor, it is not the optimum over image histories, and its intervals do not include numerical integration error.

B.4  History and Fresh-Share Ablations

The matched MAE-B and DINOv2-S grids ( and ) use fresh shares α=.5\alpha=.5 and α=1\alpha=1 (the benchmark), with temporal scale ℓ=4\ell=4 (), on HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and PassWater. HandReach/MAE-B additionally uses α=.25\alpha=.25 and .75.75 (). Each history/seed cell fits a predictor with the selected recipe above. Gains, durations, policy, query law, coordinate masks and frozen readouts stay fixed; readout recovery is rechecked on the new factual population. The same t=2t=2 anchors and queries are used across history lengths within each disturbance setting. Across fresh shares, the visited-state population and target variance change. These are ablations of the data-generating process, not same-state effects of persistence alone. Cells that exceed the no-outcome threshold remain labeled diagnostics; their physics is not recalibrated.

Appendix C Planning Protocols and Results

Frozen models and simulator replay.

Each run loads one frozen encoder, one factual-selected one-frame predictor (seeds 00–22) and the frozen state readout of ; BlueROV2 uses the 3232k-episode predictors. Nothing is fitted. The simulator runs as a separate process in the runtime that produced the evaluation cohorts, driven through its native reset, step and render calls with the evaluation configuration. In-loop encoding reproduces the stored evaluation features to within one float16 rounding step (0.0080.008), and in-loop decoded predictions reproduce the scored ones to 10−710^{-7}. For liquid transport, simulated in the SoftGym benchmark through PyFleX, the Python interface to the NVIDIA FleX particle simulator, replaying the evaluation cohort reproduces the full native state, the sources and the endpoints exactly (128128 parents, maximum absolute difference 00). Its native episode ends after 7575 native steps (2222 per transition), too early for the two prefix and three replanning transitions. Liquid transport therefore enters the one-shot and retry tasks, but not consecutive replanning; each event takes 6666 native steps.

Replanning.

Episode i∈{0,…,299}i\in\{0,\dots,299\} resets with seed 3,109,000,000+i3{,}109{,}000{,}000+i, disjoint from every collection, confirmation and evaluation range; episodes 100​s100s to 100​s+99100s+99 use predictor seed ss. After the native reset, the benchmark’s behavior policy executes the two prefix transitions, then the planner acts for three transitions. Three disturbance conditions use the benchmark disturbance σ​tanh⁡(g)\sigma\tanh(g) of , g∼𝒩⁡(0,1)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), with each environment’s bound σ\sigma: persistent, one gg per episode held for all five transitions; fresh, an independent gg per transition; and none, g=0g=0. The goal is the vector of scored coordinates reached from the warmed-up state by one command drawn uniformly from the command support, under the persistent fault, or under zero disturbance in the other two conditions. The horizon of three planning transitions keeps every episode inside the native episode limits (BlueROV2: 100100 native steps, five transitions; FetchReach: 5050 native steps); it was fixed from these limits before any full run. Results are in ; under the persistent fault, the counterfactual world model’s success barely depends on the fault size, whereas the trained predictor’s falls sharply ().

One-shot planning.

Episode i∈{0,…,299}i\in\{0,\dots,299\} resets with seed 3,110,000,000+i3{,}110{,}000{,}000+i (predictor seed ⌊i/100⌋\lfloor i/100\rfloor), runs the two behavior-policy prefix transitions and one event transition, all three with independent drivers from the benchmark law, and draws the factual and goal commands independently and uniformly from the command support. The learned and true-simulator planners rebuild the same event from these seeds, and the report checks that their goals agree exactly. The oracle planner (no outcome) minimizes the expected squared standardized distance over the driver, computed with six-node Gauss–Hermite quadrature, and uses the same cross-entropy search as the learned planners (256256 candidates, 3232 elites, four rounds); for the one-dimensional liquid-transport command, both true-simulator planners use 1616 candidates per round and run on episodes 00–9999, since each simulator evaluation takes about 1.51.5 seconds.

Same-event retries.

The replanning episodes and goal commands also define one event: the native reset, the two prefix transitions and the event transition, with drivers drawn independently per transition from the benchmark law (or zero). The goal is the vector of scored coordinates that the goal command reaches in the event. The first attempt plans with the trained predictor in both arms; each further attempt resets and replays the prefix, verifies that the scored coordinates match the event start exactly, and plans again with a new search seed, the counterfactual world model adding the readout residual of its previous attempt. The retry task was specified after the replanning results and before any retry was run. Results are in .

Planner and success criterion.

The cross-entropy search draws 256256 commands uniformly over the command support, keeps the 3232 with the lowest cost, refits a diagonal Gaussian (standard deviation at least 1%1\% of the bound), and repeats for four rounds with clipped Gaussian draws; it executes the best command seen. The cost sums squared standardized differences between the decoded prediction and the goal, using each coordinate’s standard deviation over factual outcomes of the evaluation cohort. Candidate draws are seeded by episode and step and are identical for the two arms. Success uses the true simulator coordinates: their root-mean-square standardized distance to the goal after the last step must be below 0.20.2. Intervals are 95%95\% bootstraps over the episodes of each cell, paired across arms. The one-shot ordering of holds across tolerances (); in replanning, the persistent-fault gain holds across tolerances, whereas with fresh disturbances the correction lowers success at loose tolerances ().

Appendix D Stress-Test and Model-Selection Protocols

Equilibrium prediction for the gain-fault interaction.

The analytic comparison in uses the equilibrium response below. Here TT is the centered disturbance draw, cc is the equilibrium response scale and gg is the command gain. For an equilibrium response

Y=c⁡{g​a+σ​T​[(1−λ)+λ​u]},u=a/amax,Y=c\left\{ga+\sigma T[(1-\lambda)+\lambda u]\right\},\qquad u=a/a_{\max},

with uniformly sampled normalized actions, the no-outcome disturbance variance is proportional to

m⁡(λ)=(1−λ)2+λ23,m(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{2}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{3},

while the residual-reuse error variance is proportional to 2​λ2/32\lambda^{2}/3. Hence

ρ⁡(λ)=2​λ23​m​(λ).\rho(\lambda)=\frac{2\lambda^{2}}{3m(\lambda)}. (39)

This gives ρ=0\rho=0, 0.50.5 and 22 at λ=0\lambda=0, 0.50.5 and 11, respectively.

Physical interaction screen.

For every coordinate recorded in the evaluation branches (parents ×\times disturbance draws ×\times three unequal queries, ), we compute the oracle (no outcome) R2R^{2} from within-parent conditional variances, the factual-copy R2R^{2}, the ideal residual R2R^{2} obtained with within-parent Monte Carlo estimates of the conditional means, and the interaction ratio ρ\rho (), with whole-parent bootstrap intervals; lists the point estimates. The screen uses no image, readout or fitted model; the per-coordinate values for all seven environments accompany the code release.

Fingertip readout.

The HandReach predictors of are rescored through a second frozen readout trained on factual frames for all 39 recorded coordinates (three hidden layers of width 1,024, 30,000 updates, factual-validation checkpoint selection, and the same diagnostic cohort and episode split as the state readouts of ). Two criteria fix the scored mask before scoring: simulator-only oracle (no outcome) and copy references both below 60%60\%, and factual validation recovery at least 95%95\% for both encoders. Seven fingertip coordinates meet these selection criteria, with validation recovery 95.195.1–97.6%97.6\% (DINOv2-S) and 96.096.0–98.8%98.8\% (MAE-B). On the evaluation population, MAE-B recovers all seven at 95.195.1–97.7%97.7\%, whereas DINOv2-S recovers five of them at only 93.193.1–94.0%94.0\%, so the DINOv2-S result is reported as a diagnostic. Pooled R2R^{2} uses summed squared errors and summed variances over the seven coordinates, averages single-fit risk over three seeds, and resamples parents and seeds jointly. With MAE-B, correction in feature space reaches 83.6%83.6\% on these seven coordinates, against 39.8%39.8\% for the trained predictor, −1.3%-1.3\% for factual copying and 53.0%53.0\% for the oracle predictor (no outcome); residual reuse with exact simulator means reaches 96.5%96.5\%.

Interaction-dial calibration.

The interaction dial perturbs the normalized command aa by σ​ε​d​[(1−λ)+λ​a/amax]\sigma\varepsilon\,d\,[(1-\lambda)+\lambda\,a/a_{\max}], where dd is the declared actuator direction pattern and amax=g​alima_{\max}=g\,a_{\mathrm{lim}} the declared command bound; the fault magnitude never exceeds σ\sigma, so the native no-clipping bound g​alim+σ≤1g\,a_{\mathrm{lim}}+\sigma\leq 1 is unchanged. For the equilibrium model of , matching the oracle (no outcome) target of 50%50\% with a 2%2\% actuator margin gives σ=[1+3​v​m​(λ)/0.98]−1\sigma=[1+\sqrt{3v\,m(\lambda)}/0.98]^{-1} and g​alim=0.98​(1−σ)g\,a_{\mathrm{lim}}=0.98(1-\sigma), with v=Var⁡tanh⁡(G)=0.394v=\operatorname{Var}\tanh(G)=0.394 for G∼𝒩⁡(0,1)G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). For λ∈{0.5,1}\lambda\in\{0.5,1\} this gives σ=0.609\sigma=0.609 and action gains 0.8500.850 (HandReach) and 1.0931.093 (Ball-in-Cup). Development cohorts use 256 parents ×\times 64 draws with fresh reset seeds, and all native control and replay tests pass. The λ=0\lambda=0 rows of reuse the benchmark confirmation cohorts.

BlueROV2 disturbance recovery.

BlueROV2 is rendered from a level camera with elevation −10-10 degrees, distance 1.61.6 and azimuth 9090, selected by held-factual recovery. It changes no physics, action law, reset state or coordinate mask. The disturbance readout uses 32k factual episodes (26,214 fitting anchors), with the architecture, budget and checkpoint rule above. Held-out recovery is 97.997.9, 96.096.0 and 96.2%96.2\% for MAE-B, DINOv2-S and DINOv2-B; on independent confirmation it is 97.2%97.2\% [96.3,97.8][96.3,97.8], 95.6%95.6\% [94.7,96.2][94.7,96.2] and 95.5%95.5\% [94.7,96.1][94.7,96.1]. State recovery is respectively 99.3/99.299.3/99.2, 98.4/98.398.4/98.3 and 98.6/98.4%98.6/98.4\% (held-out/confirmation). The no-outcome oracle has upper 95%95\% bound 53.0%53.0\%; decoded factual-copy upper bounds are 8.18.1, 8.48.4 and 8.3%8.3\%. For both DINOv2 encoders, the disturbance pass uses the point estimate: the lower confirmation bound is 94.7%94.7\%. The disturbance head enters neither counterfactual prediction nor its score.

Factual model selection.

The reference arm in uses width 512, the t=2t=2 fitting anchor and weight decay 10−410^{-4}. The selected recipe minimizes the mean held-out factual error over the seven data cells with MAE-B. The development grid uses MAE-B, seed zero and one frame on all seven data cells (BlueROV2 with its level camera) and varies the training anchors (the t=2t=2 anchor only, or all three recorded factual transitions of each fitting episode), AdamW weight decay (10−410^{-4}, 0.050.05, 0.30.3) and predictor width (256256, 512512, 1,0241{,}024; two blocks), with validation every 100 updates. Validation episodes and anchors are identical across the grid. The criterion is the mean over cells of the held-out factual mean squared error in raw feature units, relative to the reference recipe. Fitting all recorded transitions dominates every other factor (held-out error 44–10%10\% lower than with the evaluation anchor alone, in every completed cell), width 1,0241{,}024 is best at every training scope, and weight decay changes the criterion by less than 2%2\%. Over all seven cells, the recipe with all transitions, width 1,0241{,}024 and weight decay 0.30.3 has the lowest mean relative error (0.9310.931), ahead of weight decays 0.050.05 (0.9330.933) and 10−410^{-4} (0.9340.934) at the same width, with the largest gains on BlueROV2 and Racetrack (0.890.89 and 0.900.90). This grid is a separate development run: its reference fits use seed zero and validate every 100 updates, whereas the orig. arm of reports the original three-seed fits, so its factual gains differ from these relative errors. The final refits were launched with this recipe once it led on every completed cell and were confirmed when the remaining width-1,0241{,}024 and reference cells finished; 3030 of the 126126 grid fits (narrower widths and the anchor-only scope on four cells, worse on every cell where they completed) were not run to completion. Every arm validates on held-out factual episodes at the t=2t=2 anchor, the anchor at which counterfactuals are evaluated, so selection sees source states drawn like the evaluation ones but only their factual outcomes.

Ensembling and readout correction.

Both are computed from the same stored predictions as the single-seed arms of . The ensemble averages the embedding predictions of the three fitted seeds before decoding; readout transport applies to the decoded predictions of the factual endpoint and of the trained mean at the factual and query actions.

Pixel, feature and readout transport.

The comparison in uses the title-page boat with a uniform current, the east-west mean flow without eddies, and the frozen MAE-B encoder and state readout fitted on that collection. For 1616 fresh events and eight alternative headings each, conditional means over the current average 3232 draws shared by all headings, and a duration hh scales both the commanded move and the current. In their own coordinates, residual reuse gives interaction ratios of 1.741.74–2.182.18 in pixels and 1.921.92–2.302.30 in the 768768 features for hh from 11 to 0.050.05. Against the true position, the relative risks at h=1h=1, 0.50.5 and 0.250.25 are 5.865.86, 3.703.70 and 4.064.06 for pixel correction read back through the encoder, 0.310.31, 0.320.32 and 0.470.47 for correction in feature space, and 0.0020.002, 0.0140.014 and 0.0640.064 for correction after the readout. For shorter transitions, the readout’s own error approaches the displacement caused by the current, and every variant degrades.

Appendix E Short-Time Bounds and Assumptions

E.1  Baseline Feasibility

The benchmark thresholds of restrict which dynamics can serve as benchmarks: they fail for pure integrators () and very short transitions (), but can hold for contracting systems such as servoed actuators ().

Proposition E.1 (A continuing-integrator benchmark limit).

Consider St+1=St+At+εtS_{t+1}=S_{t}+A_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}, with independent fresh innovations of mean zero and variance N>0N>0. Past actions may use arbitrary feedback from the available past, but cannot observe their current innovation. At a continuing anchor t≥1t\geq 1, let the factual and query actions be independent draws from the same law with variance A>0A>0, independent of St,εtS_{t},\varepsilon_{t}. With V=Var⁡(St)+A+NV=\operatorname{Var}(S_{t})+A+N, the state-information Bayes reference and same-disturbance factual-copy scores satisfy

RB2=1−NV,Rcopy2=1−2​AV,V≥A+2​N.R^{2}_{B}=1-\frac{N}{V},\qquad R^{2}_{\mathrm{copy}}=1-\frac{2A}{V},\qquad V\geq A+2N. (40)

They cannot both be strictly below 0.600.60, although population residual reuse has zero counterfactual error.

Proof.

The latest independent innovation gives Var⁡(St)=Var⁡(St−1+At−1)+N≥N\operatorname{Var}(S_{t})=\operatorname{Var}(S_{t-1}+A_{t-1})+N\geq N. The query conditional mean is St+At′S_{t}+A_{t}^{\prime}, with risk NN. Factual copying errs by At−At′A_{t}-A_{t}^{\prime}, with risk 2​A2A. Both strict score thresholds would imply N>0.4​VN>0.4V and A>0.2​VA>0.2V, contradicting V≥A+2​N>VV\geq A+2N>V. The residual prediction is exactly St+1​(At)+(At′−At)=St+1​(At′)S_{t+1}(A_{t})+(A_{t}^{\prime}-A_{t})=S_{t+1}(A_{t}^{\prime}). ∎

Proposition E.2 (A contracting system can meet both baseline gates).

Let St+1=ρ​St+(1−ρ)​(At+εt)S_{t+1}=\rho S_{t}+(1-\rho)(A_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}) with 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1, mutually independent zero-mean IID actions and innovations, and variances A>0A>0 and N>0N>0. RB2=1−(1−ρ2)​NA+N,Rcopy2=1−2​(1−ρ2)​AA+N.R_{B}^{2}=1-(1-\rho^{2})\frac{N}{A+N},\qquad R_{\mathrm{copy}}^{2}=1-2(1-\rho^{2})\frac{A}{A+N}. (41)

For ρ=1/2\rho=1/2 and N=2​AN=2A, both scores equal 1/21/2, while population residual reuse remains exact.

Proof.

Subtracting the factual conditional mean leaves (1−ρ)​εt(1-\rho)\varepsilon_{t}, which cancels exactly when reused with the query conditional mean. ∎

Proposition E.3 (Small-step absolute-state baselines).

For a scalar scored coordinate SS with 0<Var⁡(S)<∞0<\operatorname{Var}(S)<\infty, let XhX_{h} and YhY_{h} be factual and same-disturbance query endpoints. Condition on an independently fitted factual predictor and the source/action pair, and write dh=eh​(z,a′)−eh​(z,a)d_{h}=e_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-e_{h}(z,a), the estimation term of (). Because the population residual error in (9) is centered under νz\nu_{z},

More factual data can reduce the second term, the estimation of the factual mean contrast, but no rate in sample size follows without assumptions on the predictor class, optimization and action coverage. Neither term, hence no duration or sample-count sweep, is guaranteed to vary monotonically in a finite experiment, and an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) upper bound on the root-mean-squared error is not a claim that the error equals a nonzero constant times h2h^{2}. A sample-count sweep holds policy, action support, representation and validation population fixed, and counts independent episodes rather than correlated frames. Very short durations can fail the benchmark’s requirement that copy and oracle (no outcome) R2R^{2} stay below 60%60\% (). Finite-duration comparisons alone do not test an asymptotic h↓0h\downarrow 0 scaling law.

The general bound is uniform and does not assert a monotone empirical error curve. If, in addition,

E.3  Estimation Error and Physical Readouts

Population baseline risks.

Fix z,a,a′z,a,a^{\prime} and take expectations under the common same-event nuisance law. Let ℛR\mathcal{R}_{R}, ℛcopy\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{copy}}, and ℛmean\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{mean}} denote embedding-space squared-error risks of the population residual rule, factual-outcome copying Yh​(a)Y_{h}(a), and the no-outcome conditional mean μh​(z,a′)\mu_{h}(z,a^{\prime}), respectively. With Δh=Yh​(a′)−Yh​(a)\Delta_{h}=Y_{h}(a^{\prime})-Y_{h}(a), the bias–variance identity gives

ℛcopy−ℛR\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{copy}}-\mathcal{R}_{R} =‖𝔼​Δh‖2,\displaystyle=\|\mathbb{E}\Delta_{h}\|^{2}, (49)
ℛmean−ℛR\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{mean}}-\mathcal{R}_{R} =2​tr⁡Cov⁡(Yh​(a),Yh​(a′))−tr⁡Var⁡(Yh​(a)).\displaystyle=2\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{h}(a),Y_{h}(a^{\prime}))-\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}(Y_{h}(a)). (50)

For the second line, expand Var⁡(Yh​(a′)−Yh​(a))\operatorname{Var}(Y_{h}(a^{\prime})-Y_{h}(a)) in (10). Thus the population residual rule always weakly improves on factual copying in this space, by exactly the squared conditional mean action effect. It improves on the no-outcome mean when the shared-event covariance is large enough. In an additive response family, the latter gain is the disturbance variance and residual risk is zero. In general the second gain can be negative: reusing a negatively correlated or greatly amplified factual residual can be worse than ignoring it. These are population identities in the modeled coordinates, not guarantees for a fitted mean or after a nonlinear physical readout. For a fitted mean, the nonnegative contrast-estimation term below reduces the gain over factual copying, and a comparison against its own fitted no-outcome prediction must also account for that prediction’s mean-estimation error.

Fitted-mean error.

Let a trained mean be fixed independently of the scored events, and write eh=μ^h−μhe_{h}=\widehat{\mu}_{h}-\mu_{h} and R~h​(a)=Rh​(z,a,ε)−𝔼νz​Rh​(z,a,ε)\widetilde{R}_{h}(a)=R_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon)-\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}R_{h}(z,a,\varepsilon). Conditional on its training data, the exact error is

T^R−Yh​(a′)=R~h​(a)−R~h​(a′)+eh​(z,a′)−eh​(z,a).\widehat{T}_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})=\widetilde{R}_{h}(a)-\widetilde{R}_{h}(a^{\prime})+e_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-e_{h}(z,a). (51)

For fixed z,a,a′z,a,a^{\prime} the first term is centered, which gives the exact bias–variance decomposition already used in ():

𝔼νz​‖T^R−Yh​(a′)‖2=tr⁡Varνz⁡(Δh)+‖eh​(z,a′)−eh​(z,a)‖2.\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{z}}\|\widehat{T}_{R}-Y_{h}(a^{\prime})\|^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{z}}(\Delta_{h})+\|e_{h}(z,a^{\prime})-e_{h}(z,a)\|^{2}. (52)

Common mean errors cancel; unrelated errors at the two actions do not. To claim O⁡(h4)O(h^{4}) squared error for a learned predictor rather than the population rule, its mean-contrast error must itself be O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) in root mean square. Consistency at a fixed hh does not supply a uniform joint limit in sample size and hh. This distinction matters when feature normalization depends on the time step; the stated rate is in fixed encoder coordinates.

Fixed disturbance scaling.

The short-time limit also fixes the disturbance law and action bounds. Increasing disturbance amplitude as hh shrinks can make the remainder constant depend on hh and remove the claimed rate. For example, replacing ε\varepsilon by ξ/h\xi/h in the squared-encoder example of changes its residual MSE from order h4h^{4} to order h2h^{2} for fixed nondegenerate ξ\xi. Strong-noise benchmark qualification and short-time approximation are separate requirements; neither supplies the other (recall and ).

Readout error bound.

Let QQ denote the query population and ηh=‖eh​(Z,A′)−eh​(Z,A)‖L2​(Q)\eta_{h}=\|e_{h}(Z,A^{\prime})-e_{h}(Z,A)\|_{L^{2}(Q)}, and suppose the frozen readout π\pi is LπL_{\pi}-Lipschitz on a region containing the true and predicted embeddings. If κh=𝔼Q​‖π⁡(Yh​(A′))−s⋆⁣′‖2\kappa_{h}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}\|\pi(Y_{h}(A^{\prime}))-s^{\star\prime}\|^{2}, where s⋆⁣′s^{\star\prime} denotes the true scored coordinates under the query action, then

‖π⁡(T^R)−s⋆⁣′‖L2​(Q)≤Lπ​4​C2​h4+ηh2+κh.\|\pi(\widehat{T}_{R})-s^{\star\prime}\|_{L^{2}(Q)}\leq L_{\pi}\sqrt{4C^{2}h^{4}+\eta_{h}^{2}}+\sqrt{\kappa_{h}}. (53)

The bound follows from (16), Lipschitzness and Minkowski’s inequality. For a pooled R2R^{2} denominator VQ=𝔼Q​‖s⋆⁣′−𝔼Q​s⋆⁣′‖2>0V_{Q}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}\|s^{\star\prime}-\mathbb{E}_{Q}s^{\star\prime}\|^{2}>0, it implies

RCF2≥1−(Lπ​4​C2​h4+ηh2+κh)2VQ.R^{2}_{\mathrm{CF}}\geq 1-\frac{\bigl(L_{\pi}\sqrt{4C^{2}h^{4}+\eta_{h}^{2}}+\sqrt{\kappa_{h}}\bigr)^{2}}{V_{Q}}. (54)

Apply this separately to each coordinate for a macro-average of coordinate R2R^{2} values. A high factual readout score does not establish Lipschitzness off the image manifold or a small κh\kappa_{h} on a shifted CF population. Nor does the absolute O⁡(h4)O(h^{4}) squared-error rate directly imply an R2R^{2} rate: VQV_{Q} may also shrink with hh. With fixed-source disturbance variation of order h2h^{2}, the corresponding normalized error can be only O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}). Subtracting the same observed factual endpoint from both prediction and truth does not change squared prediction error; outcome-error and ITE-error MSE are then algebraically identical, though differently normalized scores need not agree.

Nonlinear readouts.

π​(μh​(z,a))\pi(\mu_{h}(z,a)) need not equal 𝔼​[π​(Yh​(a))∣z]\mathbb{E}[\pi(Y_{h}(a))\mid z], even if the embedding mean is known exactly. The squared-loss theorem for embeddings () therefore does not make the decoded deterministic predictor the squared-error optimum in physical coordinates, and we report the oracle predictor (no outcome) separately (). For a simple algebraic example, let Z⁡(a)=m⁡(a)+εZ(a)=m(a)+\varepsilon with ε∈{−1,+1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,+1\} equiprobable and let π⁡(z)=z2\pi(z)=z^{2}. Then π⁡(𝔼​Z​(a))=m​(a)2\pi(\mathbb{E}Z(a))=m(a)^{2}, while 𝔼​π​(Z⁡(a))=m​(a)2+1\mathbb{E}\pi(Z(a))=m(a)^{2}+1. An exact embedding mean therefore retains a decoded mean error, although residual reuse recovers the same-noise Z⁡(a′)Z(a^{\prime}) and hence its decoded outcome exactly. This example concerns the loss/readout distinction, not an observed benchmark result. Likewise, a readout can discard non-additive feature variation, so accurate decoded counterfactuals do not establish additivity of the full embeddings, and near-additive physical coordinates alone do not verify () in the chosen feature representation.

Correction after the readout () instead uses π∘μ^\pi\circ\widehat{\mu} as its physical predictor. Its action-contrast error includes the mismatch between this decoded predictor and the physical conditional mean. The feature-space bound above does not directly bound this different construction.

Feature-space counterexample.

Let the physical outcome be x⁡(a)=m⁡(a)+εx(a)=m(a)+\varepsilon with bounded centered noise, and use the fixed smooth encoder ℰ⁡(x)=(x,K​x2)\mathcal{E}(x)=(x,Kx^{2}) and readout π⁡(z)=z1\pi(z)=z_{1}. Residual reuse with the exact conditional embedding means has encoded error

TR−ℰ⁡(x⁡(a′))=(0, 2​K​[m⁡(a)−m⁡(a′)]​ε).T_{R}-\mathcal{E}(x(a^{\prime}))=\bigl(0,\,2K[m(a)-m(a^{\prime})]\varepsilon\bigr).

The physical readout is exact for every realization, while feature MSE is 4​K2​[m⁡(a)−m⁡(a′)]2​Var⁡(ε)4K^{2}[m(a)-m(a^{\prime})]^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) and can be arbitrarily large. This establishes that the two observations are mathematically compatible; it does not establish that the pretrained representations in our experiments implement this construction.

E.4  Counterexamples

The first two are the multiplicative-fault and aliasing exceptions of (the gain-fault stress tests of measure the former); the third shows that a smooth encoder attains the stated order even for exactly additive physics.

Multiplicative disturbance.

In one dimension, s˙=a​ε\dot{s}=a\varepsilon is smooth and can use an IID, action-independent, centered disturbance draw. Nevertheless Yh​(a)=s+h​a​εY_{h}(a)=s+ha\varepsilon, μh​(s,a)=s\mu_{h}(s,a)=s, and residual reuse errs by h⁡(a−a′)​εh(a-a^{\prime})\varepsilon. Its MSE is h2​(a−a′)2​Var⁡(ε)h^{2}(a-a^{\prime})^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon), rather than O⁡(h4)O(h^{4}). This model violates the action-independent instantaneous-effect assumption, not the exogeneity of the random draw.

State aliasing.

Let the physical state be (x,v)(x,v) with hidden v∈{−1,+1}v\in\{-1,+1\} equally likely, let x˙=a​v+ε\dot{x}=av+\varepsilon, v˙=0\dot{v}=0, and observe only z=xz=x. All maps are smooth and the disturbance effect is additive and action-independent. With centered noise and actions independent of vv, the encoded conditional mean is μh​(z,a)=z\mu_{h}(z,a)=z. For s˙=a+ε\dot{s}=a+\varepsilon, 𝔼​ε=0\mathbb{E}\varepsilon=0, and ℰ⁡(s)=s2\mathcal{E}(s)=s^{2} on a region where the source is determined by its features, direct calculation gives

Scope.

The theorem concerns the population rule. For a trained predictor μ^h=μh+eh\widehat{\mu}_{h}=\mu_{h}+e_{h}, (16) adds 𝔼​‖eh​(0,1)−eh​(0,−1)‖2\mathbb{E}\|e_{h}(0,1)-e_{h}(0,-1)\|^{2}, so a uniform O⁡(h4)O(h^{4}) bound on that term preserves the rate and a uniform o⁡(h4)o(h^{4}) bound the sharp constant; no sample-size, optimization or readout guarantee follows. The optimality is asymptotic and worst case: on the hard pair the midpoint beats residual reuse at every finite hh, by 4​C4​h6/(1+C2​h2)4C^{4}h^{6}/(1+C^{2}h^{2}), so other transports can be better on particular systems; what is excluded is a uniformly smaller leading constant or a uniformly o⁡(h4)o(h^{4}) error over the class. The information model allows any amount of unpaired data generated with fresh disturbances, but not repeated observations of the same disturbance within the query event, paired alternatives or a known coupling, each of which can supply the missing information. Finally, the bound covers the smooth additive-channel class of (); multiplicative faults, contacts and aliasing remain outside it, and so does the pose-only rate of . More restricted scalar, monotone or known-mechanism classes can be counterfactually identifiable.

Appendix F Physical Calibration and Numerical Checks

Physical selection.

No encoder, probe, residual predictor or transport score selects the benchmark physics. A finite physical search declares the reset law, task-directed behavior policy, coordinate groups and uniformly random factual/query commands before scoring, and new parents then confirm the selected condition, with every terminal case retained. The scored source is the same t=2t=2 anchor after two genuine native transitions; changing a future model’s history length must not change this population.

Fresh-disturbance reference.

The environment configuration exposes the fresh (IID) share of the Gaussian driver’s variance, its temporal correlation length, action gain, bounded physical disturbance scale and number of native controls held per transition; the native integration step is unchanged. The benchmark uses a fresh share of one, so its current driver is independent of the complete physical source state and history. Conditional integration over the fresh driver is therefore an information-matched full-state k=1k=1 oracle (no outcome) reference, neither a trained predictor nor a prediction at zero disturbance. With persistent disturbances this full-state reference no longer matches the information of an image-history predictor; the reference used there is described in .

Calibration targets and replay.

For every prospectively retained coordinate, the target is a marginal 95% parent-bootstrap interval of the oracle (no outcome) R2R^{2} inside [.42,.58][.42,.58] and a factual-outcome-copy upper interval strictly below .60.60. Numerical error enlarges both intervals, which are marginal, not a simultaneous all-environment confidence claim. We also measure same-disturbance action influence directly as 𝔼⁡[(sjcf−sjf)2]/Var⁡(sjcf)\mathbb{E}[(s^{\rm cf}_{j}-s^{f}_{j})^{2}]/\operatorname{Var}(s^{\rm cf}_{j}), which equals one minus factual-copy R2R^{2} on the same population. Independent native replays check complete simulator state, intervening query steps, branch order, command/gain equivalence, held-control duration and episode stopping, with zero measured discrepancy for the selected confirmation cohorts.

Status of the numerical checks.

The references of Racetrack (heading and lane offset) and Push-T (pusher position) are analytic, with formal numerical-error bounds (below). HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and PassWater pass the image recovery criteria of with DINOv2-S, DINOv2-B and MAE-B, as does BlueROV2 with the disturbance readout of ; Racetrack and Push-T fail them and serve as diagnostics. For HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and BlueROV2, independent numerical refinements of the Monte Carlo reference agree, but we have no formal bound on its numerical error. PassWater has a bounded glass-position reference and full native replay, but only four native disturbance draws per source state, below our design minimum of 64.

Scope.

Calibration uses simulator outcomes and optimizes neither a learned model nor a difference between methods. The suite uses bounded actuator and position-goal disturbances and scores observable actuated coordinates. These choices can favor approximately affine responses; they do not represent arbitrary contact or fluid dynamics. The 60%60\% baseline thresholds define benchmark eligibility.

Disturbance process.

The declared Gaussian driver and bounded physical offset are

gt=1−α​b​(t/ℓ)⊤​ξ+α​ηt,εt=σ​tanh⁡(gt),g_{t}=\sqrt{1-\alpha}\,b(t/\ell)^{\top}\xi+\sqrt{\alpha}\,\eta_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}=\sigma\tanh(g_{t}), (57)

where ξ\xi is an episode-specific standard Gaussian coefficient vector, ηt\eta_{t} are independent standard Gaussian innovations, and bb is a fixed unit-norm Fourier basis. Its covariance is the actual finite-basis covariance (1−α)​b​(t/ℓ)⊤​b​(t′/ℓ)+α​𝟏t=t′(1-\alpha)b(t/\ell)^{\top}b(t^{\prime}/\ell)+\alpha\mathbf{1}_{t=t^{\prime}}; we do not replace it by an ideal radial basis function kernel. The fresh share α\alpha refers to the Gaussian driver’s variance, not the variance of its nonlinear bounded image, and at α=1\alpha=1 the temporal scale ℓ\ell is inactive. A realized physical offset is held fixed throughout a transition and across all its factual/query branches. This models actuator/control disturbance, not hydrodynamic wind or current.

The action gain, offset bound σ\sigma, and number of held native steps are fixed independently of the later fresh-share and history sweeps. The selected triples (gain, bound, held steps) are HandReach (1.145558,.473978,4)(1.145558,\allowbreak.473978,\allowbreak 4), Ball-in-Cup (1.472860,.473978,16)(1.472860,\allowbreak.473978,\allowbreak 16), FetchReach (.939167,.54,8)(.939167,\allowbreak.54,\allowbreak 8), Racetrack (.308,.112,1)(.308,\allowbreak.112,\allowbreak 1), BlueROV2 (1.472860,.473978,20)(1.472860,\allowbreak.473978,\allowbreak 20), PassWater (1.088889,.5,22)(1.088889,\allowbreak.5,\allowbreak 22), and Push-T (1.472860,.473978,4)(1.472860,\allowbreak.473978,\allowbreak 4), and the configuration files of the code release retain full precision. Native integration time steps are unchanged; these held durations are not equal physical times across environments and are not evidence of the asymptotic small-time regime of . FetchReach and PassWater use position-goal offsets, Racetrack a lane-goal offset and Push-T its pusher goal offset; HandReach, Ball-in-Cup and BlueROV2 use their declared actuator/thruster interfaces.

Collection and branching.

Each independent episode starts from the declared native reset law and runs two actual disturbed policy transitions before the anchor. Policies are the HandReach inverse-kinematics controller, a Ball-in-Cup policy pretrained with deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), the FetchReach reach controller, a Racetrack lane follower, the BlueROV2 goal controller, the PassWater water-transport controller and a pretrained Push-T diffusion policy, with the declared exploration. At the anchor the factual command is independently uniform over the fixed support, and evaluation uses the same factual-command law and three independent uniform query commands. No equal-action reconstruction row enters a CF score, and no difficult contact, terminal or small-action case is removed to improve a score; terminal handling follows the declared absorbing convention.

Training collection writes only the single factual continuation; branching from the identical complete simulator snapshot and reusing the realized offset occur only in evaluation. Rendering is isolated by native replay, so refreshing renderer kinematics cannot change a subsequent behavior command. Recorded prefix states, commands, disturbances and endpoints are checked against the independent evaluation sampler. State labels remain private to calibration, replay checks and evaluation-head fitting; the world predictor sees only frozen frame embeddings and observed commands. The BlueROV2 camera change () affects observation geometry only, and verifies that its factual state/action/disturbance arrays are unchanged.

Numerical references.

Push-T’s kinematic pusher obeys an affine position/velocity/goal recurrence; the independent formula matches all 262,144 confirmation endpoints within 3.42×10−133.42\times 10^{-13} pixels, and its R2R^{2} numerical bound is 1.84×10−51.84\times 10^{-5}. This concerns the pusher, not the contacted block. The frozen behavior policy improves block-goal distance on confirmation, while its block-overlap interval on that subset includes zero. Racetrack composes the native lane controller and bicycle map on the initial straight. Support checks cover controller saturation, each lateral integration substep, lane boundaries, and separation from the retained traffic vehicle over all current disturbance values. Monotone Gaussian-bin enclosures give a confirmation R2R^{2} error bound of .002697.002697, and native endpoint agreement is within 2.85×10−142.85\times 10^{-14}. These bounds include conservative floating-point padding, not formal verification of numerical libraries. The PassWater coordinate is glass position; native fluid motion is present but not the checked output. Its task controller improves transport distance while retaining 99.8845%99.8845\% of the water, versus 99.9784%99.9784\% for uniform commands. None of these restricted results establishes additive block-contact, fluid-particle or image-embedding dynamics.

Restricted-coordinate oracle.

Let IkI_{k} contain exactly the last kk retained physical-coordinate vectors, the intervening observed commands and the query command; this differs from fixing the complete native simulator state. The recovery mask defines the scored outputs, not all information contained in an image embedding: features may retain useful information about unselected physical coordinates. Thus the exact IkI_{k}-conditional optimum is not automatically an upper bound for an image-history predictor unless the required information inclusion is established. Likewise, a complete-state reference upper-bounds achievable R2R^{2} only when its information, possibly augmented by the observed history, is sufficient for the queried outcome; in particular, IID current noise does not by itself make omitted source velocities irrelevant. For a sufficient larger information set JJ and any fixed IkI_{k}-measurable predictor gg, conditional-expectation projection yields

𝔼​‖Y−𝔼⁡[Y∣J]‖2≤inff​Ik​-measurable𝔼​‖Y−f⁡(Ik)‖2≤𝔼​‖Y−g⁡(Ik)‖2.\mathbb{E}\|Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid J]\|^{2}\leq\inf_{f\;I_{k}\text{-measurable}}\mathbb{E}\|Y-f(I_{k})\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\|Y-g(I_{k})\|^{2}. (58)

For the fully fresh Push-T pusher, the independently checked recurrence of the native proportional–derivative (PD) controller is Y=q​p+cv​v+cg​(256+216​γ​a′)+216​cg​ϵ​(1,−1)Y=qp+c_{v}v+c_{g}(256+216\,\gamma a^{\prime})+216c_{g}\epsilon(1,-1). The admissible position-only predictor drops cv​vc_{v}v, and its excess risk relative to the complete-state conditional mean is exactly cv2​𝔼​‖v‖2c_{v}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|v\|^{2}; current velocity is used to evaluate this bound, never as an input to that predictor. This encloses the optimum for all three position-history lengths. On the fixed confirmation parents the coordinatewise R2R^{2} brackets, including the Gaussian-moment enclosure and conservative arithmetic padding, are [50.7973,50.8008]%[50.7973,50.8008]\% for pusher x and [51.3517,51.3552]%[51.3517,51.3552]\% for pusher y. These narrow numerical/information brackets are separate from the wider whole-parent sampling intervals, and say nothing about the block dynamics or the failed disturbance recovery from images.

For fully fresh PassWater, current glass position is sufficient for the retained coordinate: the audited scalar recurrence gives the conditional mean ρ​x+(1−ρ)​(.575+.825​γ​a′)\rho x+(1-\rho)(.575+.825\,\gamma a^{\prime}) exactly, and extra history cannot improve that conditional mean under IID. Its confirmation oracle (no outcome) R2R^{2}, given the retained state, lies in the numerical bracket [50.1968,50.2258]%[50.1968,50.2258]\%, obtained from the independently checked monotone Gaussian-bin enclosure of 𝔼tanh(G)2\mathbb{E}\tanh(G)^{2} and a propagated ratio-error bound; the separate outer-parent 95% envelope is [47.32,52.65]%[47.32,52.65]\%. This assumes the stated conservative floating-point padding and is not machine-verified interval arithmetic. PassWater still has fewer native disturbance draws than our design minimum, so its sampling intervals remain wide. Neither bound transfers to temporally correlated disturbances, which require integrating the disturbance law conditional on the permitted history. Restricted-coordinate oracles for HandReach, Ball-in-Cup, FetchReach and BlueROV2 are not computed; for these environments the reported oracle uses the complete simulator state and is therefore a stronger-information reference.

Under one behavior policy, A=SA=S with probability .9.9 and A=−SA=-S otherwise, so both actions have positive support and 𝔼[Y∣H,A=a]=.8a\mathbb{E}[Y\mid H,A=a]=.8a.
